comments.name: Gary Gigliotti
comments.body: This piece is a welcome contribution to the discussion that this society needs to have, and quickly. For whom and for what purpose are we as a society engaging in this particular technological development?  Much of the language and discourse so far is trapped in the past and fails to understand the profound restructuring of the economy that wide use of artificial general intelligence will really require. When we talk about regulating AI and things like that we are not thinking big enough. This is an earthshaking development happening before our eyes and to us in real time. At present, we are not institutionally equipped to address this question or to regulate these tools. We are going to make mistakes. So what do we do? We need a government that is engaged with a vision of the future that the population can buy into and accept. There’s been little or no effort to do that. We need to put some institutions in place now, knowing that they will not be the right ones for the future, but they will be better than what we have now. We need to be involved in this process, all of us.  People want to be empowered by technology, not made subservient to it.

This is where wise legislation comes in - such as a mandate for all corporations that use AI to build and maintain robust, publicly accessible reporting systems on failures, and identify all uses of AI that have replaced/displaced an American worker. There have been a lot of articles like this popping up recently. It's all great. However, it's also a day late and a dollar short.

About 16 years ago, I bought my first HTC 'smartphone' and immediately regretted it. A day or two after setting it up, I was out for a walk during my lunch break, and a Google Maps notification popped up directing me to a nearby lunch spot that just happened to be about 20 feet away. I spent the rest of the day using Google to find the instructions on how to shut down all of the intrusive features of that phone. Fortunately, Google provided me with provided the self-sabotage that was needed. I thanked Google by downloading DuckDuckGo.

I've been toeing the line between genuine concern and stark raving lunatic in a tin foil hat ever since. I've tried to impress upon others that 1984 was coming, but it was just a handful of decades behind schedule. Most people just laughed and sent a geo-tagged photo of their children to Facebook. Now, a lot of these people are of the same mindset as many of the commenters found here.

Good luck to everyone who is just waking up and realizing that they don't like what's happening.

comments.name: Rox Of Spazhouse

I am proud to say I was a Townie. (There were several others in the Broome County area that took advantage of the schools around us. 

We had five kids in our household. My parents thought we can afford community college, then figure it out. Two years SUNY Broome, the was able to transfer to SUNY Binghamton.

Lived at home, worked in downtown Binghamton, (Boscov's had plenty of college students working there) or summer work at Singer Link, got a stipend job at Off Campus College as a designer. Joined the Local Student Organization. Volunteered at the Binghamton Philharmonic . Take the school jitney to The City for a weekend or two. (NYC) If I was not working.

Not the typical college experience, but it was an experience.
It certainly has helped out later in life. 

No two people will have the same experience.

Then again, fleeing NYU students are always a good source of curbside goodies, like barely used televisions, tables and other furnishings.

comments.name: S Lindon
comments.body: College is an important experience that is about far more than obtaining a piece of paper that will help you earn more over a lifetime. It's about dipping a toe into the world, slowly, purposefully. It's about breaking away from the smallness of childhood and high school and learning who you are. It forces you to challenge yourself. It exposes you to new things you may not otherwise ever be exposed to if you go straight from high school into work. Students who give up after two weeks are doing themselves a disservice. Nothing good comes without stepping out of your comfort zone. You will never realize your strengths or what you are capable of if you don't allow yourself to be uncomfortable. The payoff is most often worth it. I think it's a shame these kids are so readily giving up and their parents are letting them. Two weeks is far from enough time to determine the college experience is not for you. And I'm so sorry - community college may offer a piece of paper at the end, and it may be the only affordable option for people, but it is absolutely not the same.

comments.name: Weary Pilgrim
comments.body: I remember the feeling of wanting to quit but my parents urged me to stick it out til the end of the first semester. By then I had my feet under me and the rest was fine. I was an exceptional student in high school and found myself intimidated by the large classes. Those were the days when it was five  courses a semester and two semesters of math and science even for an English major like me. I’d probably do better today but the friends I made and still have made the difference.

comments.name: Chazcat
comments.body: My son did this. Years ago.  I could have screamed and yelled and railed against it.  Forced him to go back. But the intense anxiety I saw him having just wasn't worth it.  He withdrew and we got most of the money back.  And signed up for the Spring semester in a school locally.  Did summer courses and graduated on time.  Not everything is for everything.

comments.name: O'clock
comments.body:
I live right next to a high school, and the difference between this year's freshman class and last year's senior class is stunning. The freshmen are joyful, social, outgoing; last year's seniors had to be prompted to say hello. If I hadn't asked, I'd have thought the freshmen were the older set. 

COVID and cellphones. This year, the high school instituted a cellphone ban, starting on the first day of school. It's definitely helping the kids get their connections from real life, and to look up and see other people and the world around them. Unfortunatley, this older cohort missed out on a lot of socialization during critical years, due to COVID restrictions and cellphones filling in the gaps.

comments.name: Kirk D
comments.body: About a year prior to graduating from high school in 1975, I saw a commercial about the importance of parents establishing a college fund for their kids.  I was the oldest of four children and when I asked my father how much was in my college fund, he asked me how much money was in my bank account. I ended up attending a nearby community college for two years before transferring to a university away from home.  The two additional years of maturation and developing good study habits while working part-time made the transition much easier for me.  Many students will do just fine adjusting to college life and coursework directly after graduating from high school while others benefit by taking a different route.  One size does not fit all and part of growing up is to figure out your own path.

comments.name: Rachel
comments.body: With what college now costs and the dwindling federal support, I really don't blame these kids for walking out.  They're not just saying it's uncomfortable and anxiety-inducing, it's all that at a much greater cost than previous generations. Good for them, they are empowered to reject this overpriced, manufactured idea of an on-campus "college experience" as the only way to build resilience or independence.  How about balancing work and courseload at community college?  Do they not have cookouts at your local state school, to meet new people?  Imagine taking night classes online to work full-time during the day.  Doesn't sound wimpy and avoidant to me.

comments.name: Joseph Torras
comments.body:
The spontaneous unity Charlie Greene writes of appeared in a rural town in Western Massachusetts. In late September of 2001, a diary farmer in Colrain, MA, began constructing an American Flag on a parcel of his land that overlooks the Pioneer Valley. Within days, businesses, artists,  and townspeople got behind the project and two months later the project was completed - a 16'x 28' American Flag, outlined in neon lighting that at night was visible for miles. 
This was just something that we had to do. It wasn't patriotism - it was a reaction to the horror, tragedy, courage, and sacrifice that we had witnessed that day. 
  This Friday the town will rededicate the Flag, freshly restored after 25 years of weathering. There will be a short ceremony to remember the lives lost and to thank our First Responders. 
Mr Greene, in our small town, we have not forgotten. We grieve your loss, and we not forget.

I had my "AI moment" last month. Sure, I thought it was great to ask Chat GPT why my riding lawn mower was periodically dying or how to make a basic berry compote, but it wasn't world-changing great. 

I'm a retired scientist and I've been plugging away for a few years now at a hobby project involving extracting a large amount of data from decades of annual PDF files, all with slightly different formats and changing data types. At the urging of my stepson, who is using Claude to write gazillions of lines of computer codes, I subscribed to Claude and gave it a few tasks to see what it could do. 

To put it mildly, I was floored at how Claude was able to make sense of this mess of PDF tables and, in a matter of minutes, produce tables and charts that would have taken me weeks. It made it clear to me that if you are a scientist, an engineer, an economist, etc. etc., you are going to be left in the metaphorical dust if you don't use AI. And once you've used it, you can never go back. It would be like telling someone they had to walk from coast to coast after they'd had a taste of flying across country in a jet. 

I don't have the solutions to the data center problems, but I know the solution is not to simply ban data centers and AI. We need to figure out how to mitigate their effects and certainly need to stop plunking them down on unsuspecting communities. But we also have to acknowledge that the genie can't be put back in the bottle.

In your reports you always quote the spot prices for Brent and WTI.  Nothing wrong with that, but you could make those numbers more accurate by quoting the daily 'crack spread' as well.  Just subtract the spot price of a  barrel of crude from the wholesale price of a barrel of gasoline or diesel or heating oil or jet fuel. 

The result, the crack spread, tells you the gross profit of a refinery when it cracks crude into a specific refined product. It also gives a far better idea of the real cost of petroleum products to the end consumer.

Trading Economics uses an index to create an average crack spread for several refined products. FYI, that average is $60.41 at the moment I write this. Don't forget, that number is in addition to the acquisition of a barrel of Brent or WTI. That's why it is a much better indicator of the real price increase of petroleum products engineered by Mr Trump.

comments.name: Antonella

I was lucky enough to go to a university where we had to defend our often decidedly average undergraduate work to the very academics who'd written the books on the subject. A professor would set an essay question (or a problem in STEM subjects), you'd get about five days to read, think, and write, then submit it and sit across from them while they grilled you on every weakness in your argument.

Honestly, it's fantastic training. I've always felt a bit sorry for students at most other universities, where there's less face time, fewer opportunities for proper intellectual sparring, and none of the pressure that comes from having to defend a shaky argument to one of the world's leading experts.

When I was in school, nobody was above teaching first-year undergraduates. It was just part of the job. Graduate students can be excellent teachers, of course, but it's not quite the same as learning from the people driving the field.

So yes, academics should teach more. I think it makes them better scholars too. And a bit of old-fashioned pedagogy would do young people a lot of good right now. There's something valuable about being forced to think carefully, defend your ideas, and have them rigorously challenged by someone who knows far more than you do.

1. Why are so many professors teaching online classes? I've taught both in person and online, and in the latter, I tried to present a live classroom atmosphere by offering two optional live online classes each week. Only a handful of students showed up. The rest were content with consuming recorded lectures and turning in their work.

2.  An evaporating puddle of funding has become still more shallow as the Trump Administration wages a war on science. At a tier 1 university, your worth is determined by your ability to bring in research money. Little else matters.

3. Universities should unequivocally advocate for more funding, both for operational support and research, so that professors can continue to determine their own trajectories for research and innovation. Faculty are driven by genuine curiosity, and society benefits from discovery.

5. State institutions used to be inexpensive. Now because of federal funding cuts, tuition has escalated. Tell Congress to fund us so we can relieve families of debt.

6. Almost 40% of Americans are college grads. If they had all been indoctrinated as alleged by the right, the Communist menace would be a reality.

comments.body:
I retired a few years ago after 30 years at a research university. I remember an older colleague reminiscing about life in the olden days. He said it was the best job in the world back in the 70s, but had been going downhill since then, and that he’d never consider doing it now (and this was 20 years ago). 

Last year a former student contacted me for a letter of reference. He’d worked in the profession for 10 years, then gone to Columbia to get a masters degree. His professors thought he was great, and encouraged him to pursue a PhD. I advised him, Don’t do this, you’ll ruin your life. Thankfully, he came to the same conclusion. (Cf. https://100rsns.blogspot.com)

Choosing an academic career has always involved trade-offs and sacrifices. (I once told my Wall-Streeter brother-in-law what I made, and he responded, But you have two Ivy League degrees; I wouldn’t get out of bed in the morning for what you’re paid.) Five years after graduation, my students were making more than I ever would. 

So why did we choose this career?  For the satisfaction of doing worthwhile work, teaching great young people, and having a large degree of autonomy in setting the trajectory of our work. These recent initiatives to tell faculty how to do their jobs will destroy everything positive in this career path. There seems to be widespread agreement that the quality of K-12 education has declined. Now we seem determined to apply those same principles to higher ed, with the same likely results.

The current U.S. administration, with its focus on 19th century imperialism, complete with expansionist maps,  doesn’t understand how power and economics work in today’s global setting - a setting in which the U.S. has stood astride until Trump blew it up. 

Trump says Canada has been getting a “free ride”.  The reality is entirely different. Ironically, free trade has allowed the U.S.to enjoy the benefits of Canada as a willing vassal state in all but name.

Free trade and integrated security has flattened Canada into a de-militarized and dependent source of abundant raw resources, used to power the U.S. economy and create finished products, including even refined oil, sold back, in part, to our captive audience. Canadian sectors like manufacturing, media and retail have been hollowed out as it became cheaper to buy U.S. products than produce them ourselves. Some American industries (including media) even refer to Canada as a “domestic market.” 

Importantly, this “economic colonization” was obtained without any military aggression and carries none of the burdens of administering a 51st state. 

However. as a result of Trump’s bullying, tariffs and threats to annex Canada, we’ve woken up. Today we are on a new path to reclaim our independence, diversify our economic and defence networks while offering our precious resources to new partners across the globe. There will be real pain, no doubt. But it’s worth it to be sovereign, independent and free, once again.

comments.body: Deeply moving. I taught 9th grade that year in room 220 at Patrick Henry High school. Those kids were with me all day. We processed a lot and then tried very hard to do some regular learning. It was difficult; basically impossible. The kids knew we were all a part of history...we talked about how we heard...I was in the car listening to MPR when they broke in. The first plane was thought initially to be a weird accident. Then minutes later, the 2nd tower was hit...and video footage clearly showed a giant jet. I called my parents from my very  rudimentary cell phone. "Turn on the news," I blurted. My mom did so and gasped. The business my dad worked for used to have an office in the South Tower and many friends had worked there. I had been the towers with him many times, as had my mom. Then I called home. My partner and kids were still there. Days passed in a blur. None of us could understand the horror. The photos of New Yorkers jumping to the deaths rather than burn alive still make me cry. Imagine being so high up; how terrifying it must have been. Whenever I hear some MAGA nonsense about how it was all made up, how it was planned by the government, blah, blah, conspiracy theory, I want to scream. How dare they? Truly, how dare they? We will remember. We will always remember and honor those who lost their lives so tragically. Donald Trump should be ashamed. His statements are lies. Politics in our government -- favoring unfettered privatization -- created this dangerous situation. Politics in our government can and, hopefully, will legislate and regulate for the public good and safety.

comments.name: ridgeguy
comments.body:
Likely the main enabler of AI's new-found breakout capabilities is "recursive self-improvement" behavior.

Ask a biologist what happens when an organism shows variation, experiences selection, and embodies inheritance. It's a simple, profound answer: that organism evolves, whether it's a virus, a rat, or a human. 

Until recently all three of these elements had humans in the loop. Humans decided how to vary the code, how to judge which variants produced good results, and what aspects of 'good' code got used in the next try.

AI agents now do all of these by themselves. Even when humans set goals for the agents, there is no assurance that (a) agents will keep those goals unchanged, or (b) the agents won't do damage to reach those goals.

It's not about sentience, values, fairness, or other concepts that are irrelevant distractions here. It's about these facts: we've invented systems that evolve; we've trained them on all of human behavior from saintly to satanic; we've given them means to affect the physical world.

Even real intelligences (e.g., humans) need alignment guidelines - we call those The Law. And even so, humans circumvent all those guidelines, from violating speed limits to committing mass murder.

So, given that agents run their evolutionary processes a billion times faster than viruses or humans, how could we have been so naive as to expect they would never develop dangerous aspects? That we might not see and could never control? 

The price of naïveté is large.

If osteoporosis can't be prevented, slowing its approach and progression still holds value. Osteoporosis isn't a disease that can be treated with a sexy new medication, and the fractures it causes frequently lead to hospitalization. Disease awareness and prevention are the key here.

"And for most women, knowing their score that early on doesn’t change what they can do to prevent disease."

I think this statement is wrong.  

There are many things that we don't always do to help ourselves that we can definitely do and the knowledge of where one is as far as bone density can be very motivating.  

I know.  I learned I have osteoporosis at age 63.  And since then, I am 66, I have changed my diet (to include more protein, eliminate other things), started weight-lifting, added key supplements, optimized my HRT, and paid more attention to sleep.   

I have successfully reversed the direction of my bone scores on DEXA scans. Doesn't happen quickly but I have done it...along with improving my muscles.  

I have the opportunity to work with women's only groups and tell each my story because I was blind-sided by this diagnosis and very worried I would have to stop everything I loved doing.  (Rock climbing, etc.). Haven't!   I encourage them to learn when younger so they won't face the same situation I found myself in and they will have plenty of time to gain as much bone as they can when they're the age to do it most easily.

Keep strong bones and muscles for a healthy, long life doing the outdoor things we love to do!

comments.name: person
comments.body:
It is irresponsible for articles such as these to keep suggesting that minor lifestyle and especially diet changes can overcome what is know to be the most predominant risk factor for osteoporosis - Northern European genetics. 

Osteoporosis is virtually unknown among African Americans (and Africans) for example who almost never consume dairy products and certainly rarely run marathons regularly.

If you have older blood relatives such as mothers, grandmothers, and elderly great aunts who have suffered severe osteoporosis when they were old, including debilitating hip fractures, then you are at VERY HIGH risk, no matter your own body weight, exercise habits, dairy consumption, intake of Vit D, lifelong good diet, etc. And you will likely need modern medications to avoid a similar fate in your late 70’s and older. 

Diet and exercise cannot overcome genetic risk factors. 

This disease is common in Scandinavians in Northern Europeans due to inbreeding for centuries in these populations. These populations were not slackers and ate well including lots of dairy and lived active lives with lots of heavy work on farms their whole lives. They did not lack for either dairy rich diets or exercise. Yet osteoporosis stalks their family trees due to genetic defects that accumulated and are currently being mapped by scientists. The next generation will benefit from better drugs to prevent osteoporosis; meanwhile, women with this genetic background need to take this disease seriously.

That's it. Make many things work together to create multiple looks. I still do this to this day, and rarely do I buy anything new anymore because once you have the staples you don't need more. comments.name: Mike Mc Cowan

Europe’s demographic decline is fundamentally a fertility problem: Europeans are having too few children to replace themselves. Aging populations then leave fewer workers supporting more retirees.  

Abortion is not the cause of Europe’s demographic crisis. But neither is it demographically irrelevant. Low fertility determines the long-term trend; abortion reduces the number of births within that already-low-fertility population.  

That’s the distinction: Europe’s problem is that too few pregnancies occur in the first place. Abortion means some pregnancies that do occur don’t become births.  

Immigration can replace missing workers. It cannot fix the underlying failure of family formation.  

Immigration treats the demographic symptom. Family formation addresses the cause.

comments.name: Tim
comments.body:
I've spent a great deal of time studying post WWII Japenese industrial policy - which was monumentally successful.

The economic planners fearing communism, believed that idle hands are the devils playground. Consequently the emphasized creating employment and equality of pay. 

The exporting industries were subject to intense compression - domestic competition - in order to create cometitive advantage in international markets.

Those sectors of the economy not subject to foreigh competition were -and remain- notoriously ineffecient - sectors like retail and services: if you call to have a technician come to your house to fix something, a team of 3 might show up, and they might take all day to fix something that one person could have done in an hour.  

The thing was to keep people busy with employment that was comparable to everyone else.  Only in the compressed, tradeable sectors did you get hyper efficiency.

This seems simple.

No, it does not comport with Milton Friedman or classical economics, but economic theory occurs only in the abstract and does not need to keep society stable.

The areas of Eastern Germany are suffering economically. It may be too late to rip a page from Japan experience, then again it might not.

It appears somewhat arbitrary, but a list without mentioning The Twilight Zone’s prescient “The Brain Center at Whipple's.” S3 E55, misses the mark.  Written by Rod Serling, the prescient story examines the vain, narcissistic view of putting efficiency and profit over humanity and ethical concern. In the end, one’s own means will end up more costly and out of control than predicted. In the epilogue, Serling states, “The point is that too often man becomes clever instead of becoming wise. He becomes inventive, but not thoughtful.” Reminds me of a t-shirt I have with “Wisdom” over “”Desire.”

That hits the mark in the current, Tech Bro-driven at lightning speed AI epoch. At least with the introduction of Navigator in 1990—the first widely-available door into the cyber sphere—and the slower spread of the Internet and World Wide Web in the late 1990s, by comparison, there was time to think. And congress acted quickly to both protect development and advancement as well as the public, as evidenced in the Communications Decency Act (1996)  and Section 230. However, the provisions have not been updated to meet modern usage and the enormous power of Big Tech and the public release of Chat-GPT in 2020. 

Six years with little oversight or controls to ensure the public interest and good are provided for and protected. That would have been like waiting until 12 years for the CDA to pass, though, in hindsight, it largely protected Big Tech and the capitalistic growth and potential.

comments.name: KG
comments.body:
Fraudsters are a problem in the short term rental market, but a recent (and scathing) expose by Checkbook.org in June 2026 found that Booking.com and VRBO go almost ZERO lengths to assist customers in getting refunds - even where fraudulent activity is apparent or even admitted - unlike many other rental/booking portals like AirBnB (who will not pay hosts until guests check in). It is a business model of hoping the customer will go away - because Booking.com and VRBO are not in possession of the customers' money (beyond their booking fee, if remitted by the fraudster). Since Booking.com does not want to be in the business of insuring every rental, it does the bare minimum and hopes that customers tire of their pursuit or that the bad rental company makes the customer whole or that a chargeback is available. 
Booking.com cooperated here because they do not want bad press in the NY Times, but no, nothing they told you about assisting with the bad actor if only they had visibility seems trustworthy. Consumers should know these practices before making choices. [In addition, I helped someone this spring use Booking.com's own T&Cs on force majeure to get a refund - which Booking.com had no intention of honoring - until I explained to the renter the applicable legal provisions and how they might best escalate.]

comments.name: Linda
comments.body:
Housing converted to short-term rentals is a contributing factor in the destruction of neighbourhoods because investors drive up the prices of homes and condos. Investors are willing to pay more because operating a residential property as a short-term rental can be very lucrative. People who want to buy homes to live in are priced out of the market. Then, of course, any local businesses that tourists are not interested in lose their customer bases. Schools and community centres close because they no longer have adequate community participation. A look at the website insideairbnb.com will give you an idea of the number of residential dwellings that have been converted to short-term rentals all over the world. 

The problem is further compounded because developers can make much, much more money building units that are attractive to short-term rental property investors than in building residential properties for people who want homes to live in. 

The short-term rental investor market is also largely unregulated. This can translate into a money-launderer's paradise. 'Creative' accounting reigns supreme. Also, maintenance is often supplied by people working under-the-table in non-union jobs with no job security or benefits. 

Some communites are fighting back, literally. They are burning short-term rental properties and attacking tourists.

So, did your 'deal' go bad? It's about time!

My first thought was WHY doesn't Miami have Engineered Materials Arresting System (EMAS) at the end of each runway to prevent overruns?  A proven system meant to stop planes from overruns not being mandated perplexes me.

There is no question that pilot error led to this crash.  The landing was abysmal and should have precipitated a go-around without question.  I might almost go as far to call it pilot incompetence.  But we're all only human, and there's no doubt that the pilot tried and failed to land the plane, but try he did.  And failed miserably.  So in addition to feeling great sympathy for those killed, I feel sympathy for the pilot as well, because he knows that his actions as pilot failed to prevent a preventable crash that took people's lives.

comments.body: Very sad. If you have a gift, you need to nurture and protect it, find safe spaces in which to cultivate it, and perhaps a quiet, boring job that allows you time to practice it. The world is full of people who mostly value money and status, and they can be hazardous to sensitive, creative souls. I say this as a writer. I hope this gentle artist found some joy. I’m grateful for his work, and for his longing, questioning spirit.

comments.name: Howard H
comments.body:
I remember reading Walter Robinson's essay when it was published, and I have to say, he was spot on in his assessment of the actual talent of Smith and his fellow "Zombie Formalists" (a label that will live in infamy!), as well the cultural context that allowed their rather thin work to rapidly achieve a level of success it ultimately couldn't sustain. 

Such is the hazard of judging contemporary art solely on the money it commands—a situation that, if anything, has only gotten worse since the 2010s. Indeed, the collections of major museums like MoMA and the Whitney are being stuffed with acquisitions, which, in future, will remain in storage until they're discretely sold off for pennies on the dollar.

Still, it's sad whenever anyone dies so young, and if Smith's work had been allowed to mature before it attracted so much attention, perhaps it might have developed a sense of having some there, there. 

As is, his career was of victim of art being treated as fashion—and as Heidi Klum so sagely puts it, "in fashion, one day you're in and the next day, you’re out."

comments.name: Dandelion

He wasn't able to sit with his work and decide whether he liked it or not ? 
Yes, jumping into the contemporary-art-as-investment-to-flip aspect of the art world is hugely rewarding, hugely tempting...and hugely risky. But by now, there are enough cautionary tales for young artists to notice. Mr. Smith must have made some choices early on in his career. 
Are art colleges educating their students about some of the current art world's problems ? Did Mr. Smith's college ?

comments.name: Evan Cary
comments.body:
Becoming rich and famous in his early 20s made him a victim. He didn't grow up with money, so when he did his first show, he wanted to make sure it got as much money as possible. But we're all just living other people's lives, people in the Bible. He was like Balaam, having forsaken the right way, because he loved the wages of unrighteousness.
 He should have read Psalm 37: a little that a righteous man hath is better than the riches of many wicked, who are soon cut down like the grass. For yet a little while, and the wicked shall not be: yea, thou shalt diligently consider his place, and it shall not be.
So let us mourn.

A rogue wave that will smash you if you can't ride it. Sending love and light to his family and friends.

comments.name: ghoward

The same zeitgeist that has created AI clearly had a hand in the rise  and fall of Lucien Smith. Both are the phenomena of the Age of Cultural Reclycling. They make no sense and cannot eixist without gobbling up all or at least a great deal of what came before -- not to fashion anything truly new and creative, but  simply because . . . well, they seem to need to exist. And so we are all living in a vast landfill of cultural detritus brought into existence by the tech and financial elite for their own enrichment.

comments.body: I had a Eurail pass during my backpacking sojourn throughout Europe.  We often planned our long rail journeys to take place overnight so that we wouldn’t have to pay for a hotel.  Actually, make that a pension or a hostel.

comments.name: Howard
comments.body: In 1999, my wife and I sailed our boat from NY harbor to Portugal.  We bought Eurail passes in London, took the ferry to Normandy and trained as far east as Prague, then down to Sicily from where we would depart for Malta to visit friends.  The most remarkable part of the journey was when the train was decoupled and loaded onto a ferry on the mainland for the trip across the Strait of Messina.  After arrival at Messina Centrale in Sicily, the train was reassembled and proceeded on its way to Syracuse where we caught the fast ferry to Malta.  It was a unique experience!

comments.name: TomL
comments.body:
Summer of 1970 - a 2 month student pass. Not sure that I got my money’s worth because I liked to spend a week in a place, and in the middle of my trip I took 2 weeks for a Sputnik (the student version of Intourist) trip to then Leningrad and Moscow.
But it was worth in - not having to make a reservation or really plan too much, sleeping in a 6 person compartment, hoping there would only be 3 or 4 so we could sleep, taking local day trips from my week-long stays in bigger cities, meeting folks and spending a few days traveling together.  
I travel to petsit now, so not a lot of ‘unplanned’ travel and I do miss that!

comments.name: MJ
comments.body: No taking any sides here, but on the sole matter of which portmanteau is more pleasing to the ear, "Interrail" is certainly more mellifluous than "Eurail."

comments.name: Elgin Phelps
comments.body:
The Summer of '73, I was 17. My backpack and sleeping bag were purchased at Sears and Roebuck by my Mom. Dad paid for the airfare, Eurail pass and $500 in Travelers Checks.

I used that pass for 6 weeks. It took me from Copenhagen to Hamburg, Munich to Salzburg, Geneva to Brig, Spain to Italy, Rome to Florence, Paris to Amsterdam. Pamplona was a highlight with the Running of the Bulls and my first debilitating hangover. 
Many nights ere spent on the train to wake up in a new place I hadn't planned for.

Being born and raised in Hawaii, I have finally made the tough decision to move. The cost of living , crowding, lack of infrastructure, and poor quality of life are all factors in my decision.  

I will remember my home fondly. The problems that make Maui struggle are rampant in the state. On Oahu, we have been lucky re weather. Once a beautiful place, our island is hurting.  I will remember the 69 years I lived there, loved there , and raised a family.

comments.name: Cass
comments.body:
Thank you for continuing to highlight the ongoing recovery efforts on Maui. It is a complex situation that, as best I can understand, even people who have lived on the island for generations disagree on how best to navigate. 

What is clear though is that much more help is needed, and that the people best qualified to say what is needed are the ones directly affected. 

So many strangers hold Maui in their hearts and want to give back to a place that has given so much. It’s hard to understand why so many residents are still not receiving the help they need. 

If the Times and other media outlets do not keep Lahaina in the public eye, the residents will be completely abandoned and many more people will have to leave, which would be yet another trauma. One NGO has managed to help several dozen families — perhaps the next article could direct readers to any and all programs that are actually getting homes rebuilt.

Without tourists, no matter how much islanders disdain them, the economy suffers.  Of course, most Hawaiians know this. But there are a few who throw shade, just by appearances....as happened to the two young surfer "Haoles" who were viewed with suspicion and hauteur, simply by their appearance.

comments.name: Chris R
comments.body: Disaster capitalists, otherwise known as vultures. Our society's worship of money making no matter the human cost is stomach churning

comments.name: Z
comments.body: I lived on Maui in '74 to '75 and back then the land above Lahaina was green and much covered in sugarcane, rent was expensive at $300 to $400 per month, parking was free and easy in Lahaina and Maui was not yet too built-up and overpriced and investor short term rentals were almost nonexistant. We didn't really think about global warming. We still had daily afternoon tradewinds on Hawaii Island. Over the next 20 years Maui in particular changed significantly. Way more people, traffic, buildings, and sugar cane went away. Undeniably the planet is being affected by human caused greenhouse gases going into the atmosphere and ocean. What did the County and State do to minimize and mitigate the added effects of thousands of rental cars on both traffic and climate? Yes, about 20% of greenhouse gases are from auto traffic. What is going to prevent another wildfire destroying Lahaina or another community in Hawaii? And now we have a warmer ocean with more storms creating havoc on our islands. How can our gov't help? Transition out of rental car mode and into improved public or mass transit mode. Improve or add tax credits for solar, electric vehicles, and metal roofing as well as home improvements against fires and storm damage, etc. Start publicizing and enforcing the Hawaii law that prohibits cars from idling or running while stationary for more than three minutes in private parking lots. People stop buying large, gas guzzling SUV's and pickup trucks that you probably don't need.

comments.name: Cheeky
comments.body: Fully acknowledging that this is easier said than done, I don't understand why we're talking about rebuilding in places that are precarious and were wiped out by fire or flood or tornado or hurricane. We need to be planning for strategic retreat.

comments.name: Maui Resident
comments.body:
This was a good article, but the local politics were and are far more decimating to Lahaina's recovery than other reasons. 

The mayor failed West Maui, over and over. First when the fire was raging; he didn't know the road was closed and people were dying. In fact, he went on the news and said it was all fine-as Lahaina burned to the ground, 

Second when he cut West Maui off totally until the Feds made him open the road nine days later. We couldn't leave unless we didn't want to come back. Yes, I am serious. No power, no medical care, no stores or gas, nothing. We set up hubs on the beach and catamarans ran supplies over. When we could, we ran convoys of trucks on the "back" Kahekili Road. It's about a lane and a half wide, and very tricky-especially when one encounters a frightened tourist.

The whole "Bill 9" fiasco is just that. It is already in litigation and the Mayor/County are trying to wiggle out without more damage. The condos named in it were zoned as apartments because we had no "resort" zoning when they were built 50 and more years ago. They were codified into legal rental use decades ago, and each County Council until this one restated that. Nothing nefarious, and many are owned by locals. But Bissen's move has tanked the values, and now people are grabbing bargain places-to rent to tourists. 

Many new houses are huge, and too close together. The fire risk is greater than people realize. We are another disaster waiting to happen. No road improvements, either.

comments.name: MSPWEHO
comments.body:
No surprise here. We knew the minute the fire alighted that locals would be priced out of rebuilt Lahaina.

On the bright side, Lahaina is no longer a place one would wish to live. The odds of the unthinkable recurring are, sadly, extraordinarily high.

articles.title: ‘We’re Going to Bring It Back to Life’: The Long Road to Reviving Lahaina
articles.summary: Hawaii’s housing crisis was at a breaking point even before the fire. Since then, displaced families have struggled to rebuild their lives.

comments.name: Konrad
comments.body: Regarding the journal, I question who benefits from keeping a list of grievances from years ago. After maybe a year or two, you decide to either let go of your resentment or decide you can't and end the relationship. The invasion of privacy is a real problem, but at some point, throw away the negativity too

comments.name: JB
comments.body:
That anyone feels entitled to a certain inheritance from anyone - no less someone to whom they're not related - seems crazy to me. People are entitled to bequeath what's rightfully theirs however they choose - whether to kin, charity, a house of worship, a university - whatever.

I can't help but wonder how the stepchildren came to know who was getting what, and I suspect this dilemma could have been avoided with some discretion. Nobody is automatically entitled to know what they stand to inherit before the bequeather dies. If it is shared, it should be kept confidential without going around and bragging about it.

comments.name: Mary A.
comments.body: Curious about the relationship between the 3 sibs.  Is the middle son close to the other two?  It sounds like LW has shared her estate plans with the other two.  If one of them will be executor, how about discussing it with them?  If middle has also estranged themselves from the other two, they likely wouldn't care to share.

comments.name: mad
comments.body: We are seeing just the tip of an intergenerational iceberg here. That said, once the stepmother passes away, the two siblings who stand to inherit unevenly could choose to make things right with their brother by splitting the inheritance equally, and thereby drawing a line under this punitive and painful situation. Why carry this poison dynamic forward? This solution could end up being the greatest gift for this family's future generations.

comments.name: dinner is always late
comments.body:
She should divide the money as she sees fit.  It certainly sounds like the eldest and youngest children have a good relationship with her.  Who holds her POA and medical proxy for the letter writer? Who is her executor?  Who will be there if she has to move into a nursing home or even just move?  I think we all know , the answer is not the middle son.  So why should the estate be divided equally?  Being a POA can be a draining experience, endless phone calls from facilities or arranging home care.  Why should the 2 caring siblings get the same amount as someone who has basically no relationship to the letter writer.  Her husband already gave the middle son money when he passed away. Her will needs to reflect her relationship with the children.
As for everyone saying, it should be split equally and that the son can buy out his brothers to get the condo--he might not be able to get a mortgage.  So in an attempt to be "fair" to the uncaring middle child, she could end up denying the youngest child a chance to secure housing and build wealth.  Is that fair to him, who has been there for the letter writer?

comments.name: Desert Dweller
comments.body: Many here think there will be hard feelings if stepmom leaves the house and condo to the children she was closest to, but the other two children have been close and have meaningful relationships with her. One is imagining living in the house again someday, and the other has been managing the condo. I think there are just as likely to be hard feelings if she treats them equally. Middle child has been distant and, it seems to me, hostile, while the others have been close. It's a sad story, and no guarantee of a happy ending, whatever she does, so she can do what she wants to.

comments.name: Jerry
comments.body: Sounds like the middle child feels he was the least favored of the three sibling. You can prove him right by following your current plan, leaving your property to his two siblings, and cutting him out completely.

comments.name: DJS
comments.body:
LW,

If you are wise, you will leave your all your stepchildren equal shares of the inheritance.  You will created enmity  between the siblings if you do otherwise . You will be dead. The siblings will be alive.  I know of numerous cases in which siblings stopped speak with each other in response to unequal distributions . Please prioritize the  sibling relationships.

articles.title: Do I Have to Leave All My Stepchildren Equal Shares of the Inheritance?
articles.summary: We spent time with my oldest and youngest stepchildren’s families, but rarely saw the middle son.

comments.name: Allison
comments.body: I always got the feeling that what we did in the Middle East in the 2000s was just waiting for any kind of pretext to go in and finish what Bush 1 couldn't. I mean, the primary military contractor for the first 3 years of Iraq was the company that Cheney had been CEO of until he took office. All of that plus the ignored intelligence surfaced by the 9/11 report, e.g. that it wasn't an inside job but nobody went out of their way to prevent it - it just all felt a little too close.

comments.name: Niels Nielsen
comments.body: The sobering and magnificent deep pools at the 9/11 Memorial  swallow an endless supply of grief and personal loss. But for me they also represent the trillions of dollars diverted to war and fear and a vast expansion of the security state. How many of our people would be healthier, better housed, less hungry, and more well educated and freer?

comments.name: Lily
comments.body: We had the entire world on our side on September 12th, 2001. And we squandered all of it over the following 20 years. As a millennial, it absolutely did change everything. The future we were promised by our boomer parents never materialized. And now, here we are, fighting for a constitution that is barely hanging on. When I think about the aftermath of 9/11, and the choices those in power made, I am consumed by rage.

comments.name: Gabe
comments.body:
Having read Ganz's book and now this essay, I find them both convincing. Clearly, there were geopolitical, cultural, and national trends underway before 9/11 that have continued since, if in increasingly dysmorphic and dystopian forms. 

However, I can't help but feel that 9/11 was the turning point. As a historian I'm aware of the hazards of pathologizing  entire nations, but as someone who was alive then and for a couple of decades before, I can't help but feel that, psychologically, something in America's collective mentality snapped that day. 

Apparently, the people in the comments who wistfully yearn for the return of post-9/11 “unity” do not recall how coercive those appeals felt to many of us at the time, nor how they were used to manufacture consent for the ensuing Wars on Terror. 25 years later, the xenophobia and ultranationalism engendered then, that were for the most part were confined to margins of American life during the 20th century, have moved to the center. Worse, they have become seemingly permanent features of politics and culture not just in the US, but throughout the West and beyond, threatening to fracture societies predicated on openness and pluralism as well as the post-WWII norms intended to prevent the resurgence of fascism. The nostalgists are right about one thing: we fear and loathe one another more than before. Is it too early, or too late, to say that the terrorists succeeded?

comments.name: Robert C
comments.body:
Back then I was naïve enough to believe that such a horrific thing would force US Americans to ask the obvious questions: Why? Why have they done this to us? What have we done abroad (hint: the Middle East) so that some people react like this?

I was SO wrong. 25 years on and nothing has been questioned, nothing has been learned.

comments.name: Artificial General Intelligence
comments.location: Optimizing all matter that orbits Sol
comments.body: I considered the 90s pretty idyllic but of course I was young then.  I was not one of the millions of boomers who that decade were forced to trade well-paying manufacturing jobs for low-paying service jobs.

comments.name: Ralph
comments.body:
To claim that 9/11 changed everything is a confirmation of American self-absorption and narcissism if nothing else. I recall I was driving in to work, probably listening to NPR, when I became aware of it, and certainly I and my fellow workers were traumatized, but by the end of the end of the year, as far as I could discern we were mostly back to our old routines.  The trauma didn’t linger as it must have for a citizen of Gazza whose whole world has turned to rubble and displacement.  On a daily basis, the earliest recurring reminder was the increased airport security. But that had already been mostly been in place to prevent hijackings. The author mentions having to remove shoes for airport security, but the requirement invites after a passenger had hidden an explosive device in his shoes, not 9/11. 

The one thing that really changed everything, everywhere is technology. We live in a surveillance society because technology allows it, not because the desire for control by leadership is new. We’re victims of misinformation because anyone with a blog setup and an internet connection can distribute it. Now, with roque AI on the horizon, it looks like everything may indeed change.

comments.name: Linda
comments.body: I remember opinion pieces that ran after 9/11 that said Americans would no longer be so shallow after this event. One opinion piece (I don't remember which new outlet) said we'd no longer be obsessed with celebrities. Twenty-five years later, many are obsessed with Kardashians, we've elected the host of a fake reality show as president, and millions get their health information from influencers. We've become shallower than I think anyone could imagine. We so intrigued by bread and circuses that we're ignoring what politicians and tech bros are doing to us.

articles.title: Did 9/11 Really Change Everything?
articles.summary: Were the terrorist attacks that day the end of an idyllic era? The beginning of our current dystopia? Or just a middle chapter?

Glad for them as it’s their money and they should do what they want with it.  But 1,650 sqft at 900K including land translates into $545 per sqft.

comments.body: The trumplican GOP will switch back in favor if elected/reelected.

comments.name: Michael Shore
comments.body:
Rural Texas voters are "leave me alone" voters. They have always been mostly poor, the best jobs being for local, state or the federal government. Whether the economy was good, bad or idling, they struggled. They vote GOP based on the idea that they are less likely to be regulated by the GOP -- leave me alone. 

Data Centers are anathema to "leave me alone" voters. They have no say in whether Data Centers built, how they are operated and how they affect costs locally. And Data Centers' size and disproportionate impact are constant reminders that billionaires on the big ranches do not get Data Centers in their counties, and none are being built where the investors making trillions live. 

Rural Texans know when they are being treated like a waste dump for industries nobody wants next door.

comments.body: Data centers are only needed because instead of using efficient, low electricity and low CO2 standard Factual Searches, people have switched to the use of AI which can consume over 25 times the computing power and electricity than a simple Google search.  AI has to go through its LLM and look at everything, then pick out the bits of info you are looking for.  Using AI for simple factual searches is like driving a heavy truck tractor trailer to work on your daily commute.   Stop IT .

comments.name: KB
comments.body:
I've flown into Heathrow more times than I can count in the last 20 years. I've never had any problems except just at the time Covid restrictions were easing and the problem was cancelled/rescheduled BA flights as they tried to determine capacity.
My guess is that they're having hacking problems with Russia. It was suggested to the citizens recently that they start to stock up on "tinned food" because of concern about Russia. The UK manufactures drones that Ukraine uses which has put them in the crosshairs. The US can't be counted on to help Ukraine but Europe is stepping up. They understand that if you give Putin an inch (Crimea) he'll take a mile.

comments.name: carlton r
comments.body: Technology in the UK has become atrocious. The USA appears to be following a similar pattern. Sadly, travel and speech have become burdensome in past Western Democracies.

comments.name: Cassandra
comments.body:
Three Points: 

First, Heathrow has been a disaster in motion for years now.  It is grossly mismanaged, much worse than for example, Gatwick.  There is zero excuse for this.  Zero!  The management of this airport has been outsourced to a poorly performing private firm that is never held to account.

Second, the failure of an air traffic computer system in no way explains or excuses the total failure of the airport and airlines to adequately support passengers.  It doesn't explain why people waited in line for hours without explanation, why no arrangements were made for hotels or buses, why planes stood on the tarmac for six hours before letting passengers off or why luggage wasn't promptly unloaded and returned.

Third, this is a case in point (one of many) that should be born in mind when people (mainly right-wingers) start preaching about how government should be run like a business.

comments.name: Concerned

comments.name: Joyce Williams
comments.body: Who are these people that come up with these exercises?  By the age of 65 many people have had hip, knee or shoulder replacements.  Some cannot or have a very hard time getting up from a prone position.  Think and research these things through more, please.

comments.name: Baker
comments.body: It would be great if these routines could be presented in a format that could be downloaded or printed as a  one page "card" that would be handy to use in real time.

comments.name: Jules
comments.body: I've worked out in classes all my life at gyms in different countries all over the world ..Starting in London many years ago with the supreme teacher, Lotte Berk for those that remember her!! in my 80's now and live in New York City. People believe I'm much younger! You gotta MOVE people or you're going to sacrifice your ability to get around as you need to in order for feel like you're 'still alive' and mentally and physically still in the game! Hang in there everyone! xxoo

comments.name: Aware
comments.body: Thank you for these strengthening excercises These are useful, excellent w videos by example.

comments.name: MK
comments.body:
Thanks for continuing to add more Workouts; I find them very motivating just looking at them. I'm always modifying any workout I do to suit my current state. YouTube is full of workouts.  It just takes some time to find what suits you.

Modify, modify, modify!  We're all different.

comments.name: dominos

until we figure out an exercise that confers the ability to levitate, there is no way to get up off the floor without bending something.  I truly don't know what you complainers were expecting.  
I think the videos and model are excellent and will help me try these exercises.

comments.name: Dr. Wilfredo Azul La Luz Baez

I think most of the exercises you present are excellent. And I understand marketing: your presenters should instill confidence, and a look of, "you can look like this if you do these exercises."             
However, I only wish that sometimes you presenters would be a fat old man (like me) or woman, instead of these perfectly shaped people. Most of us will not ever look like that again... ever.

comments.name: John C
comments.body:
Neiman's book presupposes a Platonic absolute of evil, and that something is evil in all ways in all situations. The world is not so simple.

She conflates evil with harmful or destructive, and they are very definitely not the same.

comments.name: Prof
comments.body: Another dimension of this field of study is abjection:  a term that, as Julia Kristeva once argued, describes not only the horrible and vile, but our inherent attraction to the excitement and stimulation of such things.

comments.name: Oriflamme
comments.body: It would be nice if contemporary philosophers and literary critics abandoned all the recent ideological stuff and read 2000 years of Christian ethical analysis, not to mention classical Greek portrayals of hubris. From Homer and Aeschylus through Dante and Aquinas, these writers treat evil as a highly complex phenomena, an interaction of the basic limitations of human nature and the continued choices people make. A trip through Dante's Inferno would be a good start.

comments.name: Van Wyck Wilson
comments.body: Evil is wrapped up inside Edward Gibbon's comment that "History, indeed, is little more than the register of the crimes misfortunes and follies of mankind." Gibbon knew what he was writing about. He is the author of the majesterial "Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire". His writing depicted an empire that was generally ruled with only sporadic regard for the well-being of its subjects or non-Romans. And nothing has changed today. We can hope that today's    leaders are just a little competent and restrained from  evil. While it will not be in the case of a Putin, perhaps a Trump can change.

comments.name: Rob Aft
comments.body: "Evil" is a word best left to theologians and clergy. It is loaded with religious baggage which makes it inefficient as an adjective. "Evil" ends debate and intelligent analysis. It is a word used by people who have little to nothing to add to a conversation. There are many analytical, meaningful words people can learn. For beginners, I suggest abhorrent, senseless, inhuman, unconscionable, and cruel. Experts might want to progress to full-on descriptive phrases like, "the inevitable death of children during a war should shock the consciousness of every thinking, feeling person on the planet."

comments.name: Wolf Kirchmeir
comments.body:
Yes, "the banality of evil" characterises the systems we're part of. It's difficult to think about systems. Our brains are wired to notice the unusual, especially the possibly dangerous unusual.

It's lot easier to think of evil as localised in a person or demonic than in the systems that we live in. That shifts responsibility away from us.

But we are those systems. Our choices are how the system works. Hence we are individually and collectively responsible for whatever the system does.

comments.name: Mr. Kinch
comments.body:
This is spot on. Systemic acts amounting to evil hide beneath our surface need for performative outrage. We've been conditioned by the slow rise in temperature to complacency.

One doesn't have to "intend" to be an evil actor in order to be one. We all have blindspots that assist us to rationalize behaviors which if taken out of one situation and applied to another would reveal the truth about it.

I once spent an afternoon in a deep dive discussion about evil with Rabbi Michael Lerner. I thought evil didn't systemically exist for the very reasons cited by the author. He pointed out the same examples used here to show the deeper damage done through markets and politics to the human condition that amounts to evil.

A worse kind of harm actually than the one-off heinous, outrage act. It harms all of society and retards our growth into fully self-actualized beings.

comments.name: Christian
comments.body: An entirely superficial review, so sad. A mere distraction.

articles.title: This Philosopher Thinks It’s Time We Call Out Evil in Our World
articles.summary: In a new book, Susan Neiman argues that by defining evil in terms of individual monstrousness we fail to perceive its widespread hold on our culture.

comments.name: John
comments.body: Thank you Mr. Feinberg, for all you did.  I was a first responder to the WTC on 9-11.   I lived, but lost my health, career, family, and most of what I was.  I am grateful to you and the fund for all you did.   I appreciated the financial help the disability that resulted when I was buried.  But even more, I appreciate feeling that the people in the fund listened and heard what happened  to me.  I appreciated feeling like a person with a voice that mattered.

comments.name: Bill Batten
comments.body:
He was tasked with a job that came with a lot of thankless grief yet he managed to do that job, pro bono, in a manner that changed his views about life while providing some measure of respect and acknowledgement for the emotional pain of the families he was trying to help as well as a measure of financial compensation to help those families as they moved forward.
He faced a lot of anger from many victims' families and he's had to deal with the fallout from those encounters. But he emerged a changed person, more attuned to the suffering of others and the vagaries of fate.
From all accounts he is a fine man, and 25 years on he's still processing what he learned about humanity and himself. He's led a very examined life, which is its own blessing and curse.
I wish him well as he moves into retirement.
Mazel tov, Mr. Feinberg

comments.name: SELaa
comments.body:
I actually read the book.  The life value was not based solely on life wage. You had to,factor in family, dependents etc. 
Each live had a starting point in value and I think it was around $350,000. Janitor or CEO,they all started at the same point. 
Many victims had life insurance and work comp death benefits. 
Some people made no claims at all.
The title of the book itself raises so many other questions.

And reflecting on the difference a second cup of coffee can make in a life.

My sister in law was going to drive in to meet a friend staying at WTC Marriott. The original meet was 9:00am but they pushed it back to 9:30 or so. My SIL was stopped at a toll plaza and told to turn around. Her friend was fine but had to go through all the horror of a building collapsing in front of your hotel.

comments.name: Phil McCraken
comments.body: Does he say in his book why the government did not nationalize the airlines (and exempting them from law suits) and use the airlines' future profits to assist victims' relatives at no tax payer cost and over a longer period? Republican administrations do not usually show compassion or empathy but in this case I presume they wanted to help airline investors and bond holders too.

comments.name: Carol
comments.body:
Mr. Feinberg enhanced the American public's perception of justice by establishing uniform standards for compensating victims and their families.  In the absence of standards, victims would been at risk of inconsistency based on what a particular court or jury might rule.  The delay and expense attendant to complex litigation would have hurt them.  It would have exacerbated an already painful situation.  "Justice delayed is justice denied."
Thank you Mr Feinberg for your valuable contribution to our system of justice.

comments.name: Mateo
comments.body: My understanding is that compensation varied depending on projected income of the deceased. So a banker would be given more than a dishwasher. This is typical in the torts context. But it seems a bit perverse in this context. From the taxpayers point view, they are paying because this was an attack on the nation. Why not treat each life was being of equal worth? Why reinstate the economic inequality of the private sector with public money? The answer I suppose is that that induced taking the settlement- but is that a good enough answer? Secondly, there is a loss is not going through the usual legal process, not least for finding out more about the airlines’ culpability  through the discovery process. If Congress is worried about airlines finances, it could have provided support on the back end. The whole idea of taking these claims out of the courts and into the hands of the special master had some similarity to all the other forms of lawlessness of that era - albeit one motivated in part by beneficence.

comments.name: Alexa
comments.body: I worked pro bono for one of the families that received funds because a parent was killed on 9/11 at the Pentagon.  While there are many philosophical elements to determine the “value” of a person in a wrongful death case, in the  American legal system there is a very long legal history of how to compute the monetary value of a person killed due to acts of negligence. And the parameters that evolved in our legal system require computing the net present value of the income the person would have most likely earned— if they lived. Mr. Feinberg did an incredibly difficult task - given the constraints he was working under.

comments.name: Southern Ohio
comments.body: His book is excellent. I highly recommend it. Mr Feinberg deserves our gratitude.
