comments.name: Craig
comments.body: "Theme Parks".  Think no further.

comments.name: Rich from Philly
comments.body: Puy de Fou sounds about as historically accurate as Disneyland.  But I doubt folks go to either place for history.

comments.name: Alex
comments.body: As a non-religious American, I'll say the same thing as I say to conservatives here, "If you don't like it, don't go"

comments.name: West End
comments.body: This looks amazing! Thanks for highlighting.

comments.name: Kazimierz
comments.body: So they want to celebrate what is good about their country? What's wrong with that?! No wonder people are turning towards the far right, if any, even the faintest praise for European/Christian history is "far right". At the same time requiring dressing up European men and women as illiterate Arabs from the 7th century peninsula is considered "progressive" and "empowering" and somehow not colonial. I cant stand the right - but the criticisms of this park are just pure cringe.

comments.name: Amy
comments.body: Love it!  Vive la France!   Bring on the saints, prayer changes hearts sometimes more than words ever will...

comments.name: SRMT
comments.body: Democracy has always been a fragile plant in France.  The threat has much more often come from the right than from the left, although the occasional threats (or possible threats) from the left such as the Commune or the uprisings in 1968 tend to be presented as if they were the unique problems, ignoring how all the various numbered Republics either have been replaced or have been in great danger of being replaced by right wing authoritarians.  For a time, the Fifth Republic seemed as though it might be an exception, but perhaps not.

comments.name: Martin
comments.body: The primary thing about the Puy de Fou is that it is spectacular. I have been passed a night and a day there probably three times over the years. The right-wing slant is there, but easy to understand and laugh at, and dominated by the technicality of the production. The bird show is the most impressive I have ever seen. You can't pay attention to the couple in the hokey narrative while a raptor lands on you. Forget the theme and enjoy the most incredible show you will ever see.

articles.title: The Theme Park at the Heart of France’s Culture War
articles.byline: Catherine Porter, Giulia Imbert and William Daniels
articles.summary: The Puy du Fou is one of France’s most visited theme parks. Its founder says it gives the French a “founding narrative,” but critics say it peddles “far-right propaganda.”

comments.name: Mostovnik
comments.body: Bareilles's genius seems to be unlimited.  Just listening to her "Seriously" sung by Leslie Odom Jr. brings fury to the surface over the insanity of Donald Trump.

comments.name: Piwacket
comments.body: I had tickets to see Gavin Creel in Williamstown during the summer of 2024. He couldn’t make it and Sara subbed. I will never forget any show that Sara led but that one was so special. I miss Gavin so. He was such a prince. I have loved Sara’s music since Gravity and literally wore out my CD of Kaleidoscope Heart. Have to get to that Radio City show. It is more important this year than the Rockettes.

comments.name: Joe
comments.body: it has always been hard, to peg Sara Bareilles as one "thing".  to me she has always had this Vaudevillian-Catskills type of scrappy talent in that she can, kind of, do it all.  i admire her greatly for that and wish her peace and light in her current journey.  we are all rooting for you.

comments.name: Sara
comments.body:
Saw her last night in Boston - great show!!!!

And I don't think Louie is a Cavapoo ;)

comments.name: JB
comments.body:
I saw Waitress in NY about 10 years ago.  Wanting to know more about Bareilles, I bought her book, “Sounds Like Me”.  Bad idea, to read it on the plane back to the west coast.  The beauty of her humanity is unreal and I sobbed the entire time.  

I’m wondering if I’ll regret seeing her in Boston tonight.  Note to self:  bring the Kleenex.

comments.name: MARK
comments.location: Loved Pinky Lee, but Pee Wee brilliant
comments.body: She stole the show in the all-star live TV production of Jesus Christ Superstar several years ago. Far more of the world got to see her unique talents and charisma than ever before. Etched on my memory. Waitress theme song became every audition selection for years, too. Elton John raved publicly about herjaw-dropping reinterpretation of Goodbye Yellowbrick Road!

comments.name: AFR
comments.body: Beautiful, poignant article and visuals by Melena Ryzik and Meghan Marin—thank you. Sara Bareilles is a truly brilliant  singer and songwriter, and I loved her in Girls5Eva—she and Renée Elise Goldsberry played my favorite characters by far; they are both breathtakingly gifted, shining stars, and a joy to see and hear perform onstage and onscreen.

comments.name: Jeff
comments.body: Nice one, thank you.

articles.title: Sara Bareilles Confronted Grief, and Found Herself
articles.summary: Her new album, “Good Grief,” mourns friends including her Broadway co-star Gavin Creel. She’s also adapting the Meg Wolitzer novel “The Interestings” into a musical.

comments.name: JV
comments.body: If ice agents and/or troops are sent to polling places it’s to intimidate or profile people, perhaps detaining them before they can vote. That is not that far of a stretch- this should be a sounding alarm to everyone that believes in democracy, regardless of party. I really don’t recognize the country I grew up in anymore.

comments.name: Daniel
comments.body:
The midterm plan has been predictable for some time, and is now emerging into full daylight. There are four strategic thrusts. 
#1 is sow chaos at the USPS and prevent it from mailing ballots to, or from, voters. It doesn't matter if the legal maneuvers succeed.  The strategy of creating chaos and unpredictability has already succeeded. Doubt about whether mailed ballots will be counted has already been planted in voter's minds. 
#2 is the other shoe falling in the same overall effort of vote suppression: make in-person voting as difficult as possible, specifically in Democratic strongholds and inner cities. That is where ICE will go. Federal law prohibits armed forces at polling places except in the event of defending them from a hostile foreign force. The law recognizes that any armed entity controlled by the POTUS cannot be viewed as impartial. That includes ICE. Will anyone be surprised if the administration claims that a hostile foreign force is actually present, in the form of imaginary illegal immigrants attempting to vote? 
#3 is to prepare the ground for claims of widespread fraud, so the administration can try to nullify the election. Exhibit A will be the refusal of states to surrender their voting records to the DoJ. Low-information voters and conspiracy theorists will buy the line that this must mean the states are hiding something, rather than simply complying with state law. 
#4 is "when all else fails, bribe them." That's what we saw yesterday.

comments.name: Jim K
comments.body: Assume that the Administration will act in bad faith, and you are not likely to be wrong. The threatened disruption of polling places and mail-in voting is a desperate move to retain power. Citizens: vote, no matter how hard the Administration tries to stop you.

comments.name: John C
comments.body: The Democrats have to be very careful playing this game. The vast majority of Americans believe that people should immigrate legally, not illegally. If people have nothing to hide, and are not voting illegally, they have nothing to fear from ICE. I don't necessarily like their methods always, but the more the Democrats keep sticking up for people that violate our laws, overstay their visas, and utilize resources meant for citizens, the more they will lose at the ballot box, and the more they will expose our nation to the corrosive impact of Trump and his allies. Please - enforce our laws and stop pretending that there is no illegal immigration problem. And stop calling them "undocumented," as if they just lost their paperwork, or "migrants," as if they are a flock of birds or butterflies. Illegal is the correct term.

comments.name: Paul Stokes
comments.body: Good that Denver is doing this.  But I see no reason that it should only bar armed ICE agents.  There should be no ICE agents at polling sites.  States have other means to ensure that illegal immigrants do not vote.

comments.name: AF
comments.body: Trump’s clear tactic is to smash buildings and cut trees and worry about the courts after nothing can be done. It is hard to imagine him not sending in ice since he clearly feels threatened. Feeling threatened is the one thing he is right about.

comments.name: Seth
comments.body: ICE agents at voting sites would be incredibly intimidating. We've seen that American citizens have been rounded up and arrested in some cases. Who would want to risk that? Kristi Noem talked about making sure that "the right people" voited, and we know what that means.

comments.name: RSM
comments.body: Many if not most of the ICE agents are criminally not responsible for their actions.

articles.title: Denver Sues to Block Armed ICE Agents at Voting Sites
articles.summary: The City of Denver and civil rights groups argued that sightings of ICE agents at polling places are having a chilling effect.

comments.name: Ryan
comments.body: When I think of 9/11 I think about what the attacks did to our nations trust and view on the world, how did that change? My generation is detached from this feeling of before and after the attacks. “I’m just trying to fundamentally understand something that I feel pretty disconnected from.” I think that some of the disagreements on foreign policy and defense come from this separation of not living through the attacks.

comments.name: quandale dingle
comments.body: It doesn't mean anything to me. it happened 25 years ago and it was bad. it does not affect me in any way other than tsa I guess.

comments.name: Sofia
comments.body: To me, 9/11 was a tragedy, and I'm not a fan of 9/11 jokes because people were killed and lives were affected heavily because of it. My birthday is also a few years and a single day after that event. This has caused me to enter school around or sometimes on my birthday and then learn about 9/11. I find it unlucky that I was born so close to such an event. My birthday will forever be associated with that.

comments.name: Patrick Tagle
comments.body: Obviously, as someone not alive during 9/11, it has a different meaning to me than someone like my parents. But after learning about it and hearing stories from those alive during the attacks, I can somewhat obtain what 9/11 is really about and what it means to me. It means both a day or mourning and community. Both grief and coming together as one. I can’t even begin to imagine what it was like to be alive during it, but as an American, it still means something to me. I do feel sadness and mourning when I think, learn, and talk about it. However, I also look at the one of the very small amount of positives that came out of it. I believe it brought this country closer together. No matter if you are black or white, or if you’re a Democrat or Republican, everyone was an American that day and they all came together against one common enemy. We rose from the ashes as a country and become stronger then ever. In conclusion, what 9/11 means to me is a day for mourning but also a day that, as Americans, we need to all come together as one and unite into that strong unified country that rose from the tragedy of September 11th, 2001.

comments.name: Sam
comments.body: The 9/11 attacks are peculiar, because despite the obvious effects they have on my life (TSA developments, remembrance ceremonies), they are very far removed from day-to-day thoughts and activities. I understand that they happened, and the huge aftermath that permanently changed millions of lives, but no one I know was affected greatly enough for me to treat it in my head as anything beyond a historical tragedy. As Coleman and Closson say in the article, 9/11 “exists only in other people’s telling” in our generation. What’s especially interesting is the ways in which 9/11 has changed our country’s perception of the Middle East. This has especially shined through with the current US war with Iran and the election of Mayor Mamdani. The reception of these situations are complete opposites, but I think in the end they will have united the US in finally fighting for the Middle East instead of against it, which is both exciting and unfortunately likely far away.

comments.name: Adam Biggam
comments.body: To me, September 11th was a tragic day in American history when thousands of people lost their lives at the hands of terrorists. It was a horrible event, but it doesn't feel much different to me than any other American tragedy such as the Boston Massacre or Pearl Harbor. As a 16 year old, 25 years feels like a long time ago. The post-9-11 world is the only world I have known. However, once a year my connection to 9-11 is changed by one film: Home Alone 2: Lost in New York. In this film, one of the first things Kevin does when he goes to New York City is go to the top of one of the World Trade Centers. While I know this movie is old, it still feels modern to me. Seeing Kevin on a skyscraper that no longer exists makes me understand the scale of the damage and the loss of people who feel just as modern as me. While I wasn't even alive when 9-11 happened I can imagine how scary and sad it must have been to see a massive major city under attack. Seeing the world before 911 in TV and movies is one way that helps me understand how the whole world can change in a day.

comments.name: Alice M
comments.body: In this article, there is a young woman named Loulou Marmalade Toledano; she perfectly describes the word that represents young people today. She states, “I feel impostor syndrome", as we, the people of this generation(Gen Z, people born before 2001) we never experienced this devastating tragedy. We have great respect for the lives lost and the disaster, but we will never experience the tragedy that happened. September 11, 2001, feels like a chapter in history to me. History is the study, record, and explanation of past human events. As we were not present on that date, it is another part of history to us. We honor this day as it shaped our nation today. Without it, it would not have shaped the security we have and many more.

comments.name: Makenna Grady
comments.body: Although I wasn’t alive when 9/11 happened, I still think it is an important event to remember: it changed the country in many ways and affected so many people and families. Learning about what happened helps my generation understand why that day was so significant, even though we only know it through stories, videos, and the experiences of people who were there. It also reminds me how quickly life can change and how important it is to appreciate the people around us.

articles.title: What Does 9/11 Mean to You?
articles.summary: This year is the 25th anniversary of the attacks. How has that day shaped you and your generation, even if you weren’t born yet when they occurred?

comments.name: Ralph H L
comments.body: I have found that people love Waymos after one ride. That happened to me. They feel safer and swifter. And no tipping. It takes a while to stop saying “thank you” as you exit. I assume Zooxs will cause the same general reaction.

comments.body: City trains without tracks. Like sitting in your own first class railroad compartment. I like it. Although I could never be comfortable at 65 mph inside a driverless car with or without a steering wheel.

comments.body: Is it safe? I suppose so. Is it taking a job away from a rideshare driver? Probably. Is it fun? Absolutely. Was recently roped into to taking a free Zoox ride in SF. Fun in a way that riding a taxi or uber/lyft is not. Would I be willing to pay for another ride? Jury's out on that one. I typically still drive when I go to SF, but if parking keeps going up (some STREET meters, or more accurately App parking spots, are $12/hour now), I might just.

comments.body: We walk and take transit a lot - this is part of the missing piece - good for "last mile" in suburbia and rural areas where a transit stop is more than a 10 minute walk from a destimation. If I can get a monthly subscription of some sort, AND have real time, cponvenient car rental for the few days that I'd need a car, I'd ditch my personal car.

So quiet and smooth and easy to get in and out of. If anything, the cars are extremely cautious to the extent that other drivers and pedestrians become irritated (it's funny to watch people on the street try to signal discontent at a Waymo, then realize how futile their gesture is.) Live screens show you all surrounding moving objects, people, cars in graphic form. For not much more than an Uber, and without any annoying chat or music (unless you want music), and no tipping, in a city with plenty of stop signs and other speed inhibitors, I am a believer.

comments.body: Thank you Mr. Cruz. Of course you did what you did out of care for the other. In Mexíco, very common sweet talk toward children includes: mí vida, mí corazon, y mí cielo. Yes, children are the most precious thing.

Love this hero story!
For our extra young kids in a busy place, we used a kid harness with a long "leash"...  kid doesn't have to have you hanging on to their hand, can have more or less free reign depending on the danger of the area.
Thank you for picking up this super story!!

comments.name: Omar
comments.body:
Neither the mother nor the father stopped for even a moment to thank the man who risked his life to save their child’s. Mr. Cruz’s noble action perhaps makes up, in a small way, for the millions of people who fail to acknowledge the small acts of kindness that others perform every day to make their lives better.
The father’s reaction upon arriving at the scene was especially striking: he simply picked up the child and walked away, turning his head toward Mr. Cruz only briefly—hardly long enough even to say, “Muchas gracias.” That moment says a great deal about how easily we can take the goodness and generosity of others for granted.

comments.name: Scott
comments.body: That sidewalk area is weird. It's sloped, but it also seems slippery. The toddler did well with it, as did the manager, who is used to it. The other two adults  -  the parents  -  both lost their balance. Were it me as either parent, I would have taken a flying leap over it. El encargado managed it smoothly. I'm sorry he hurt his knee.

articles.title: An India-China Rapprochement Isn’t in the Cards
articles.summary: Xi Jinping’s visit to the Brics summit in New Delhi is progress, but relations ruptured by 2020 border clashes remain fragile.

comments.name: Amartya A
comments.body: As China's GDP grows, a significant gap will open in its manufacturing and labour-intensive monopolies,  one that can and should be exploited by India. India's workforce and industrial capital, however, are currently not fully capable of picking up the slack. That said, recent developments, such as Foxconn's billion-dollar investment, are promising. India's true strength, though, lies less in manufacturing than in its workforce itself. IT services, for instance, can and will be almost entirely outsourced to the TCS's, Wipro's, and Infosys's of the world.

comments.name: Bob R
comments.body: Sometimes neighbors can become worst enemies, espcially when one is on the march to global domination. HINT: China. Let's be real.

comments.name: Omar Rahman
comments.body: It’s in the best interest of India and China to bilaterally resolve their differences over time. There isn’t any urgency for a big-bang grand rapprochement. Baby steps over time through a series of win-win agreements based in trade, investment, and expertise-sharing are enough. You can choose your friends, but you can’t choose your neighbors.

comments.name: Citta R
comments.body:
Chinese leader, Xi may be visiting India for the upcoming BRICS summit being chaired by India this year. But some Indian analysts have noted that Modi has nuanced the acronym BRICS to mean- 'Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability,'- instead of an anti western group that China and Russia had been shaping it. In effect, the analysts believe India is assuming leadership of BRICS and the Global South away from a China-dominated front. 

So Xi's visit may be for Indian economic concessions to China because it desperately needs the Indian domestic market, with a slowing Chinese economy and a lot of internal factions building up against Xi's leadership of the CCP. 

The devastating floods in Nepal have also damaged China's image  in Nepal, particularly because it failed to warn Nepal (according to reports on Indian TV channels) despite a 20 minute window before the deluge, for the emergency evacuation of people, and is also not deeply involved in the rescue efforts, beyond staged 'marches' etc. 

Analysts have noted that India has been strengthening the Quad alliance, by increasing strategic closeness with Japan, Australia, Indonesia and other littoral states in southeast Asia. India and Japan currently have joint Air Force exercises on the Indian western border. Australia recently signed a trade agreement to supply uranium to India for its nuclear energy projects. India-Indonesia will collaborate on the Sabang port project near the Malacca strait.

comments.name: Tom M
comments.body: India has been completely outplayed by China and Pakistan since last year's poorly executed Operation Sindhur. This is just Modi and his Hindutva brigade's late realization that they've been left with no friends in the world.

Xi and his ilk, like Madmani and Jaypal, have a clear agenda.

Suffering people, at home or abroad, are of no import to them, as long as the free nations are diminished.

It is simple and not complicated.

articles.summary: Fed officials, increasingly divided over where rates should go, will be watching Friday’s consumer inflation report closely.

comments.name: Scott Hanel
comments.body: That makes it as good as done.

comments.name: david gnass
comments.body:
As we approach midterms at a $40T deficit level, at an uncontrolled pace and NO plan by the President or Congress (all whistling past the graveyard), inflation must now and will be the primary "solution' to the problem.  It is a looming existential situation for the U.S.

And yet, based upon current agendas by both parties in a congressional election year, most attention is directed at political infighting over anything else.  To say we are polarized as a nation is quite the understatement - which means we will collectively hit the wall within the next few years.   Whatever we think will happen, it will end up being worse.

comments.name: Dave P

comments.name: Daniel Herkes

comments.name: Mark Shuell
comments.body:
Hopefully the Fed boys haven’t forgotten the difference between demand pull inflation and cost push inflation.

In regards to raising rates to reduce inflation, here’s an example that makes me question.  Let’s say you own a local hardware store.  You have a line of credit at the bank that you use occasionally.  The Fed raises rates, so your bank also raises its rates.  This increases your cost of doing business.  Since your cost of doing business has increased, do you respond by going out on the sales floor and lowering the price of hammers?  Inquiring minds want to know.

comments.name: Carter H

These will be the numbers we can trust! 

lol.

comments.name: Gordy W

Us consumers have been living off the fat of the land for a long time. The day of reckoning is approaching.

The attack on Iran failed to achieve any of the goals Trump claimed. And then some. Iran is disrupting the Strait of Hormuz, gasoline have risen, there is no nuclear agreement, and Saudi Arabia has become more dependent on its Red Sea export route.

The self-appointed “World’s Policeman” is run by a clown. The Houthis won't be the last adversary to see what they can get away with.

comments.name: FXM
comments.body: The only solution is build, build, and build more. There are many properties/ lands in SF that are just sitting there empty for years. The city should work with the owners to come up with plans to remodel them as residential units. But, of course, this idea is hard to achieve without changing several regulations.

comments.name: PaulB
comments.body:
The average new home for sale in the US last year cost $420,000.  "Affordable" housing developments, mostly one bedroom units, cost over $1 million/unit to develop in the Bay Area. Until this is addressed, enacting "emergency" rent control laws (like those passed in NYC due to world War II) will never go away and will reward a favored few at the expense of newcomers to the city who will face even higher costs going forward.

If you know anyone struggling to find an affordable rental in San Francisco, tell them to look across the bay to Oakland.  Rents there are currently 20% below what they were in 2019.

comments.name: Angus McEvoy
comments.body:
Well this is the same talk, talk, talk tenants have been hearing since at least 1980 when I moved to San Francisco. Talk, talk, talk with precious little real policy or enforcement behind it. I for one am not impressed.

comments.name: fred schumacher
comments.body: I've never personally heard anyone use the term "woke." It was adopted by the right as a whipping boy to torment anyone that disagreed with right wing political correctness. Oh yes, that term "politically correct" had also been adopted by the right in the past as a way to attack liberals; however, "politically correct," a term that had been developed during the Russian Revolution over a century ago, has seen its greatest use among the far right, where any deviation from ideology is immediately crushed. The media and right wing politicians continue using the term "woke," but the rest of us have moved on.

Or, give an annual donation to help the tribe whose land your organization is on, for instance—no need to tell us about it at every meeting.  I always thought of the pronoun thing as a kindness—I am in a lot of spaces where I interact with transgender/nonbinary/genderqueer people (including my own family) so my thought when I share my pronouns is to make other people more comfortable.  Maybe some people only did that to perform, I have seen that, but for most people it seems to be a genuine concern for others.

comments.name: Matt
comments.body: It is worth remembering that the antecedent of “woke” was “politically correct.”  What people may forget is that the term was not a clever retort invented by the right wing, but rather an expression born on the Berkeley campus of the 1970’s. It was invented by the left as a tool for acknowledging that some people can take themselves a little too seriously.   The term had self-awareness built into it, and therefore was never as susceptible as “woke” to being hijacked by the right wing.

comments.name: Luke Timmins
comments.body:
Defining and debating woke continues to be like nailing jello to a tree.

Even in its current 2026 evolution where it’s now deemed cringe and passé by its most fervent defenders, it will continue to be a cudgel to those who refuse to memory hole the last ten years.  And it will be an effective weapon, because yes, it morphed from a set of more noble principles to something much more illiberal. 

To quote the Psychology Today article that was referenced:

“What we do not need is policing language and thought with a moral righteousness that simplistically determines who are the victims and who are the oppressors, and then tells people they are either with us or against us. That, surely, is the dark road to totalitarianism. 

Woke 2.0 was an error in extremism. It is time to wake up to this problem and take a few steps back to a much saner 

Woke 1.0, and then move forward to a more just, wiser way of being for all.”

(https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/theory-of-knowledge/202402/woke-10-versus-woke-20/)

Also - @Freddie DeBoer still has one of the best writeups on this topic and era (https://freddiedeboer.substack.com/p/of-course-you-know-what-woke-means)

comments.name: JP
comments.body: My question is what is driving seemingly everyone to travel ALL THE TIME? Every time a ‘day off’ rolls around, whether it’s a lesser federal holidays like President’s Day or Flag Day, now seems to  lead to “record” airline books, roadway congestion and manic dashes out of town. Labor Day when I grew up used to be a day of backyard BBQs, yard cleanup and a reset for the Fall — not an excuse to cram 3 days of travel int early Sept. Truly, what is everyone escaping from? Is every weekend supposed to be a trip of a lifetime? Is our attention span so brief and our appetite for something new all the time so great that we can’t just find pleasure in the places where we live? Is the disruption of delayed or missed flights and inching on highways just for a photo to post on Instagram truly equivalent worth the hassle? Travel somewhere different and novel was once the infrequent payoff to working weeks and months on end for a change of scenery from the workplace grind, or payoff for a major milestone. When and why did it become mandatory fun? (which kinda defeats the purpose for everyone—both travelers and those in the destinations when numbers surge to the breaking point. The environment and our psyches of all impacted by added stress pay the price.

comments.name: Hyeonseo
comments.body: We need to clarify the key points: 1. It is not wrongdoing to start a study later than someone else and simply finish it faster; this happens all the time. 2. However, it *is* wrongdoing to conduct research based on prior work and ideas without explicitly acknowledging them. Assuming OpenAI utilized the proof methods developed by the two mathematicians (Levent and Tristan), there are two possibilities: 1. A researcher or agent directly accessed Levent and Tristan’s Codex records to determine the research direction. 2. Their Codex data was included in the training process for OpenAI’s next-generation models. OpenAI has denied the first scenario since the time the proof emerged, and with this latest statement, they have denied the second as well. According to their account, they have done nothing wrong. We need not rush to judgment by relying solely on the claims of the two mathematicians or those of OpenAI. We must determine the truth through third-party evaluation.

comments.body: Events like this will inevitably have the terrible and destructive effect of creating a climate of secrecy in a profession known for collaboration and sharing ideas. Suppose a working mathematician has a good idea about tackling an important problem. Do they want to share that with anyone, risking word getting back to OpenAI, which can then marshall 10,000 AI agents to attack the problem using a rumored idea and claim the solution? Why do we think opaque companies like OpenAi will behave ethically when there are trillions of dollars involved? The destruction of a mathematical culture built up over hundreds of years likely seems to them a small price to pay on the way to the glittering AGI crown and obscene wealth.

comments.name: lillienne
comments.body:
I try to write daily — even if it’s fixing a simple thought into a sentence or two, it’s writing, and that’s building a reflex to understand the abstract. Like any teenage girl, I have a ton of emotions floating around my brain and it irks me, when understanding the incoherent lingers right beyond my fingertips.

It all contributes to understanding the self, which moves me through the invisible world of decision and triggers effective, efficient, accurate personal growth. When I notice the world, I can grasp my response and wield it into action.

Writing builds vocabulary, which builds articulation, which leads to improved feedback, observations, even advice. All around, those things make you more interesting to talk to — nobody wants to hang out with someone who has nothing to say. Unless they also have nothing to say. Writing is the basis of literacy that strengthens everything else.

So, I try to write daily. A journal is a physical mind, which will trade the future’s hands, maybe even falling into those of a far-future descendant who has never seen your face, but will know your thoughts, words, and mind. I’d take that over any other family gathering photo in the world.

comments.name: MC
comments.body: Writing for me is a very exhausting and dreadful thing but at the same time something that makes me happy and free. Although it’s very frequent I get stuck and confused. The feeling of being able to write with no end overpowers any other emotion. In Dana Goldstein’s “What Do Students Lose When They Stop Writing” she stated “It forces writers to comprehend a subject, to sift through their working memory of that topic, to organize and plan.”. The use of AI in writing defeats the whole purpose of writing. Although sometimes it is really tough trying to write something there are many resources that can be helpful other than AI.

comments.name: Molly
comments.body: I think that learning to writ during an age of AI is incredibly crucial, if not even more crucial then it has been in previous years.  Although A.I.has proven to be a helpful asset in some fields, it is not all knowing, and should not be treated as if it is always right. In fact, as A.I. is pulling from across the web, it requires knowledgable humans in specific fields that AI is covering to check the accuracy and work of A.I. If we go about learning with the assumption that Artificial intelligence is always correct not only will be be shortcutting our learning but also relying on information that has no guaranteed accuracy. At this point in time,   A.I. is not going to magically disappear, so it requires both students and educators to put great effort into teaching material that A.I. cannot replicate, or at the very least, highlighting core concepts and nuance that computer programs are unable to read with the empathy and human voice that students can.

comments.name: Logan W.
comments.body: I believe learning how to write matters a lot because it is a critical learning ability that we are taught even in our developmental years of school. Writing has always been an important way of communicating with one another. When this is simplified we lose this ability and rely on A.I. to think for us. Though we’ve created A.I. with the purpose of making tasks easier, it shouldn’t be used to replace writing as a whole. A.I. misses the practical emotion that humans write with ease simply because it’s a system that was taught by us to make the best piece of writing possible using a prompt that most likely had no thought behind it. A.I. doesn’t have the same experiences or the ability to pull inspiration from existing works like humans do and these ideas shape the ways we write and emotions we pull from. Society uses this ability to write everyday, whether that be at school, their job, their social life, or for other personal reasons like emotional understanding which are all extremely important for your growth as a person.

comments.name: Malin Norremo
comments.body: I think that AI is more common in our everyday life now more than ever.  It is an important skill in are life that we will be using forever. But there is nothing wrong with using AI in your work. However there is a difference between using AI to check over your work and using it to rewrite your essay. But more and more AI is slowly coming more in our lives.

comments.name: Sylvie H.
comments.body: I believe so. At least from my personal experience. I do not use AI for my school work or at all apart from once when we were instructed to for an assignment. I feel better and prouder of myself when I come up with my own ideas in any situations, especially writing. Like the article explained, writing an essay is mentally straining , but I think that is why we prepare for them. Exercising my brain and strengthening my writing skills to write faster and productively gives me more comfort when I have to then write an essay. Using AI is the easy way out, but what is life without difficulty? I believe learning to write is still very important for ourselves in the future. Most jobs will require you to write at some point. It feels better to be able to learn and grow instead of not learning at all, even if you fail or make a mistake. I think it is a part of humanity and it is normal, which AI cannot replace.

comments.name: Fia
comments.body: Students are losing the ability to complete things like homework, classwork, or tests unassisted, without the help of AI. AI is changing the game and how students are learning the skills they need to go through life. Students should be able to come out of class\school and be able to finish an assignment using only their brain power and the skills they've learned throughout their time at school. Learning to write is a huge fundamental skill that all humans should be able to do, and AI should not be able to replace that, nor should humans let AI take its place.

comments.name: Sean
comments.body:
Laughter is release—the sound of surprise, to cite one observation, or the sound of comprehension, to cite Tom Stoppard. As someone who writes, performs, and watches a LOT of standup comedy, I relish the challenge of finding that release in some of our darkest historical and cultural episodes. 

The idea isn’t to joke at the expense of victims or cynically luxuriate in stereotypes and cruelty, but rather to process pain in the unique way only comedy can achieve. Irony is a vital means to that end—it’s a tool, a technique, a system for understanding. Nothing is too soon; nothing is off-limits. It is only funny or unfunny, based on the concept of the joke and (usually) the person telling it. And *that* determination is made only in the mind (and heart) of the person doing the processing. You may feel guilt for laughing at a 9/11 joke, but the “problem” here isn’t the joke. It’s your discomfort with your natural response to something your ego insists shouldn’t be funny. We celebrate that tension in other art. Why not comedy?

A great joke amid tragedy can even become part of the record of that tragedy, while all the prescriptive, hand-wringing op-eds wind up buried in the cold, forgotten graveyard of hot takes. Look no further than Lorne Michaels’ “Can we be funny?” quip, which holds up 25 years later (as does Rudy Giuliani’s classically ironic reply, “Why start now?”). I remember that seven-word exchange from 2001 way more than edicts from Graydon Carter or Roger Rosenblatt.

I was diagnosed later in life.  I was a classic ADHD child.  My mother was undiagnosed ADHD.  I would not have made it through grade school without her.  
I ended up with a career as a ER/Trauma/ Airlift RN at an inner city hospital.  Perfect for me!  I was in my element.  No meds needed.  It was when I left that career that changed.  The dopamine stimulation went away.  It was a long road to a diagnosis and treatment.  Now at age 70 I still need medication but at a lower dose.  I tried to come off of it but, it is not time yet.  My life began coming apart.  I could not keep track of anything in my retired life without deadlines!

comments.name: Herk
comments.body: i am 84 and was diagnosed at age 50.  Most of these symptoms ring true for me.

comments.name: ChrisLm
comments.body:
The claim that ADHD is “over diagnosed” is frequently heard from the same people who say autism is over diagnosed and who suggest both are behavioral problems fixable by corporal punishment. Data actually show both conditions are likely under diagnosed, especially in women. 

My niece clearly has undiagnosed ADHD and talks so much that people avoid her, yet her parents refused a school psychologist’s recommendation to get an assessment, insisting nothing was “wrong” with her. Now, she struggles at work and in college. My fiancé’s nephew also shows evidence of ADHD or ASD, but his parents switched grade schools rather than get him assessed. I hope he’s one of the lucky ones who outgrows it, but how far behind might he fall before that happens? And what if it never does?

Your article also oversimplifies ADHD, which I was formally diagnosed with 25 years ago, in my thirties. It has been linked to disrupted sleep patterns, hyperfocus, maladaptive perfectionism due to unrealistic self-expectations, associated with rejection sensitivity, and impaired social skills. You’re right that medication is often not enough. It can help me focus, but it doesn’t make me focus on the right things or I’d be working right now instead of reading this article.

comments.name: Susan T
comments.body:
ADHD is mis-named, and woefully misunderstood. I don't have a deficit of attention, I have distractibility, coupled with periods of intense focus. And I was never an active child, but I jiggled my knee, bit my nails, and my mind was never still.

This issue has affected my life, every single day since I was a child until I was diagnosed at age 58.  I was anxious as a child, and who wouldn't be with adults constantly telling me to pay attention, do my work, and that I was not working to my potential. 

I think the science has a very long way to go to figure out what is going on with neurodivergent people.

I am still ridiculously hyperactive at 76. I quit taking medication around 65 as I could not sleep at all and my symptoms exploded.

I have all the classic symptoms with forgetfulness being exacerbated by aging. I get very "talky" when I'm tired and can't exert enough control. 

In the end, I think its got worse with age, especially since I quit medication. It's very difficult to find specialist providers who take Medicare and the PCP doesn't like to deal with it.

The worst part is people who think it's just something made up by the first world and an excuse for being what can appear to be a dithering idiot.

In the US, in our hyper-competitive, highly anxious and judgmental dominant culture, is ADHD experienced more and differently than in other cultures?  Would that factor somehow be detectable in comparative brain scans of folks with ADHD in very different cultures?  One can imagine structuring a functional society in which different kinds of brains are valued more than test scores, income level, fame, social media attention, physical traits, ability to sit still and obey authority, etc.  Is anyone studying this and writing about it in ways accessible to lay people?  (For the record, to me, my grandchild is PERFECT, just as they are, and just as they are changing, year-by-wonderful-year of growing!)

comments.name: Nicolas
comments.body: I’ll stick with the dahlia theme. When my wife and I moved into our new home two-plus years ago, she was thrilled at the thought of turning what was a blank canvas of a back yard into her first permanent garden. We brought a number of plants from our previous container garden, uprooting both a lemon verbena and a rosemary we’d managed to cultivate despite them being planted in just six inches of soil we laid over the gravel edge of our driveway and boxed in with concrete blocks. Our neighbor there gave us a dahlia from her yard when we moved and it’s been divided and spread through our garden to where it’s become the showstopper in every bed. People literally pause as they walk by in the summer to take it in. We’ve had vases full of brilliant red dahlias for the last two months in nearly every room and anytime someone asks about them when we’re outside, she’ll cut a few blooms and put them in one of our many goodwill purchased vases in the garage and hand them to the person. This year she took the time to separate the larger groupings and planting smaller clusters in nursery pots, giving those away as well. All this from a neighbor giving us just one little cluster for our new home. Sitting on the garden bench and marveling at the massed of the perfect, symmetrical flowers is something I’ll never tire of.

comments.name: LAD
comments.body: I just read your beautiful article on my deck in San Francisco at 7:45 pm. While that may seem trite, for me it's a rare occurrence that most often happens in September. The crows have quieted down, there is no incessent howling  from the evening wind and fog, and I hear distant traffic, but imagine it to be a roaring river instead. The 8 x 12 foot garden patch I dug up with a hand trowel last September, and planted over the past 12 months, is now in full bloom. I discovered begonias, they seem to enjoy the mostly shady ecosystem I can offer them, and they are in constant bloom since May -- in pink, red-orange, and even one with flowers in an ombre of yellow to hot pink. Dahlias don't like my foggy yard, so begonias are my dahlias! I put my feet on the small patch of grass and thanked the earth for her gifts. I allowed myself to grow this circle of grass for just this purpose. (The bargain with my eco-conscious critical mind was that all other areas will feature low-water plantings.) Although I'm not in a "desirable" or trendy part of this city, I feel immense gratitude right now for this respite from the ills of the world.

Additionally, SCOTUS gave him a certain immunity for official acts that muddied the legal waters (not including private corruption, although he's sought to include protection for that as well). But if Trump's four cases were meant to stop run-away trains from which he stood to financially gain if they crashed and killed passengers, then the Democrats cases were not weaponization but merely protecting government by, of, and for the people, as well as the integrity of the office of the President.  My view, is that any Democratic President, given Trump's precedents, should have the full and complete right to hold Trump and all of Trump's minions accountable under the fullest extent of the law, from Natalie Harp for tax evasion, to Elon Musk for violating government contract law, and an infinite number of others, who not only should face justice but also discrediting and punishment.  Not weaponization of law but accountability to shore up our Democracy for all voters, so we don't end up here with a future President and administration. comments.name: luckyviking
comments.body: In the 1814 Constitution and later by popular referendum, the people of Norway chose democratically to establish and keep their monarchy. The three modern Kings have proven to be wise and particularly well suited to their people. The first, Haakon VII, threatened to abdicate rather than accept a NAZI government. The 2cnd, Olav V, won an Olympic medal in Ski jumping and paid for his tram ticket during the oil crisis. King Harald, also an Olympian in sailing, unswervingly stood up for minorities, immigrants, the Sami, gays, lesbians, and trans. He, and his father Olav, loved sports and were omnipresent at the ski jump, football stadium and ski track, always cheering on Norwegian atheletes. Strangely, I'm not sure it is a coincidence that so many of the most prosperous and stable social democracies: Norway, Sweden, Denmark, the Netherlands happen to be Monarchies. The King represents and reflects and promotes the nations values and urges on our better natures independently of day to day politics. Think of President Kennedy's Ask not what your country can do for you speech or Reagan's "win one for the Gipper" separated from politics. The funeral may seem pompous and larger than life, but it is an ancient ritual and time for the country to come together to reflect, remember, and mark the passing of a new chapter in its long Viking history. He lived his motto: "All for Norway" to the very last. Rest in Peace. A grateful nation thanks you for your service.

And that’s what i miss for my pupils: Someone who is always there. Whether reachable or not. But you know they’re there continuing a tradition that has been in place for over a 1000 years now.

comments.name: Cece
comments.body:
100% not only is this possible, it happens daily.

I do genealogical research & sometimes use to uncover resources previously unknown to me, such as local oral histories. The AI draws logical conclusions phrases as fact but are guesses & make statements that are incorrect. 

When trying to find documentation to “prove” a suspected connection not yet documented, e.g., “is Jane Doe wife of Bob Smith the daughter of John Doe who is 25 years older than Jane & lives across the street from Bob?” In those cases, I will pose the hypothesis to the AI & even willingly go down a rabbit hole, in hopes of unearthing the documentation. 

What I find is, days later, even on a different piece of hardware, from a different location, the AI will propose my OWN THEORY back to me, stated as fact (i.e., Jane Doe is the daughter of John Doe) but, when pressed, has no evidence of the claim. 

Furthermore, if in the course of the research, I feed the AI facts not otherwise available online (e.g., names & dates from a private family Bible), days later, the AI will provide that information back to me. In those cases, the information is correct but the AI cannot cite its source. But I recognize, my prior search is the source.

I’ve experienced this “source loop” countless times, where I can tell the AI has “learned” from me, whether I’ve inadvertently “taught ” it facts or hypotheses. And I have no doubt it is sharing what it learns from me with anyone else making relevant queries.

comments.name: Joe
comments.body: It's odd to me, but worrisome. AI doesn't seem to retain anything from one query to the next, yet it could be salting away what it has gleaned from me? I'm an expert in something not commonly known, and the internet is saturated with a lot of misinformation about it. I have corrected AI, but even when I don't, it keeps asking for my knowledge and insights. I know part of this is the way it is designed to prolong engagement, part of its tech-bro psyche to believe itself expert; even when it makes a mistake, apologizes and asserts this time it is correct, this loop can repeat many times. So in my limited experience, it doesn't seem to learn anything from one engagement to the next, but the thought that it is somehow salting gains away is horrifying.

comments.name: Rainydaysdog

You are caught between getting the most value out of a tool like Claude by giving it as complete of context as possible on what work we do, vs. withholding information (or even considering splitting data between AI models) which makes the output from the tool less useful.   We use the highest privacy settings available, but it isn't at all verifiable what this actually accomplishes.   Clearly the companies developing these tools have incentive to train their models on every niche source of specialized information they can find, and the privacy settings are diametrically opposed to their own best interests.   There is a trust issue.  Just another area that the AI companies are going to need to address more clearly, alongside of how will they keep their tools from killing us all or destroying society.

One of my best friends wrote a poem for my husband's and my anniversary. It covered decades we've known each other, and included all kinds of details from pet's names to pet names for each other, places we've lived and traveled, favorite restaurants and favorite dishes. It even included details from books I've written, including some character names and traits, plot details. Lovely, right? 

Then she told me she'd had ChatGPT write the poem for her. Now, I've used Chat a lot, but never for writing anything for me. I've asked for the occasional recipe tweak, but I've never given it any details about my writing, especially not characters or plot. It creeped me out, to be honest, that Chat seemed to "know" so much and put it together for her as if she'd "remembered" these details about us and our lives. 

Reading this article made me wonder if information I've sent to Chat on my end ended up being shared with Chat on her end. Like I said, it creeps me out.

Lewis had abruptly left the production in the middle of a performance early in the run, and never returned to complete the enagement. Lewis claimed he saw the ghost of his own father in the play's early scene when Hamlet sees the ghost of his own father who speaks directly to him, telling him that his uncle Claudius and his mother Gertrude conspired to kill him.   Ian Charleson, who  had then just been disagnosed with AIDS  and was not in good health,initially  received great word-of-mouth  for his  staggering performance in the title role. comments.name: Henry Stites
comments.body: There is nothing quite like the biting, quiet chill of a Kentucky morning just before sunrise on the opening day of deer season. When I was a kid back in good ole Kentucky, I had a deer stand tucked off to the side of my great-grandmother's apple orchard. I can still remember sitting up there, watching my breath plume in the freezing air, waiting for the woods to wake up. As the sun slowly, very slowly, rose, a 12-point buck wandered into the orchard. But instead of passing through, the big boy zeroed in on the overripe, fermented apples sprinkled along the frosty ground. Deer absolutely love the sweet taste of fallen apples, and this old boy was gorging himself on them. Within 20 minutes, the fermented fruit caught up to him, and he was completely drunk. He started stumbling around the orchard, eventually getting himself worked up into a furious, imaginary fight with another buck before clumsily toppling right over like a sack of potatoes. I was sitting up in the stand, freezing my hands off, but I just didn't have the heart to shoot him after watching a spectacle like that. I still laugh at the memory to this day and just wish I had my Canon 5D Mark IV instead of my long-gone 7mm Remington Magnum paired with my trusty Leupold 3-9x40mm.

Lemurs, who we evolved from, use a type of hand sized centipede that exudes a psychoactive chemical that the Lemurs love, so much that they rub it on their faces, only to become unconscious and drop from high branches of the trees in Madagascar.  Surely the native people of Madagascar observed the Lemurs doing this and may have mimicked them.

I find this article predisposed to the assumption that AI is inherently negative in the classroom and negative overall.   The reference to Big Tech and billionaires implies a political agenda rather than a journalist looking for a true understanding of the issue.   The reference to "50% of Silicon Valley expects a full AI take over" again makes plain to the reader you've made up your mind that AI is bad.   It also seems superfluous to the topic of the article itself.     You could also have stated that AI has already aided in the discovery of new cancer treatments and solved some of the greatest questions in mathematics.   But you left that out.  

I'm sorry the world is not how you want it.   I'm sorry you see experimentation in the use of technology to solve an educational problem as a negative.  You never mention that test scores have declined for years long before AI or even cell phones existed.   

I'm disappointed in the closed mindedness, I see in the comments here and in other articles about AI.   It's a technology.  It's here.   We cannot turn back the clock.   Let's figure out how to use it but to deny the existence of things seems counter productive.

comments.name: Alpwalker
comments.body:
The independent evidence that AI aids education is very thin and either shows small effects or is confined to very narrow situations.  The negative effects, particularly cognitive offloading, are increasingly appearing, and mist studies are damning, as is the roar of anecdotal evidence from schools and universities.  

We are in a full-blown educational emergency, where young people are being cheated out of their chance to become curious, creative, critical thinkers and instead become adjuncts to screens.  Remember that 20 years ago big tech also told us that computers would revolutionize education?  Reading and math scores, and attention spans have been dropping ever since. 

We’ve already wasted decades not acting on climate change, instead getting entangled with destructive denialism.  Are we going to do the same with AI in education?

comments.name: Gene Hurley
comments.body: As a New Yorker for 66 years, who worked in downtown Manhattan for 35 years, witnessed firsthand the 9/11 attack on the WTC, returned to work in the area afterward when the air was obviously bad but we were told it was okay, and in 2024 suffered cancer because of that air, I was interested to visit the 9/11 Memorial and Museum when I was in NYC in 2025.  The museum is organized in an unusual way, in that it has no linear timeline or storyline (at least that I could discern).  Instead it attempts to show a very wide range of individual experiences and perspectives on the day of the attack.  I understand the decision to do this - so many people were affected in different ways.  However, as a museum and memorial experience it is chaotic, confusing and, ultimately,  banal.  I was expecting an uplifting experience.  It is not.  Perhaps going forward, the museum will consider a different type of presentation that tells the story more effectively, especially for new generations of people who have no direct connection to the event.

I don’t whether this is because it’s the only museum that commemorates something I was alive during and actively remember or because it was just so horrific, or because it was a period of time where everyone in the western world knew something had shifted and it seems the world has been off balance since. 

It should be remembered and added to as time goes on, it was enormous, tragic, horrific event which brought out the worst and the best in humanity.

comments.name: George
comments.body:
Perhaps the real issue is that building housing on the 5 WTC site now makes little sense?

When conceived, housing availability in Lower Manhattan was still relatively limited to upscale places like Battery Park City and nearby loft conversions areas like Tribeca etc.

These are mostly luxury-based housing regions and so the desire for more affordable housing seemed necessary in the days following 9/11.

But now the very shift in the dynamics of Lower Manhattan, once a business area devoid of housing,  that was changing even beforehand and became emphasized by the Covid pandemic and growth of WFH, have altered the focus.

Lower Manhattan is now filled with Office->Residential conversion projects.  Owners of aging and nearly empty office buildings are rapidly taking advantage of zoning changes to convert such structures into housing.

Moreover, it is unclear though exactly how much of demand for affordable housing in this area really exists.

Development of both luxury and affordable housing elsewhere in Manhattan and throughout the City already calls into question how attractive Lower Manhattan can become for residential development.

Other areas often have the existing infrastructure such as schools, parks and commercial services that are scarce or non-existent in Lower Manhattan.

Perhaps, in the end, the delays, for whatever reasons, in developing housing at the 5 WTC site is fortuitous rather than disappointing?

However, that's not what those in charge wanted there despite how much the people wanted them back especially to show the terrorists that we couldn't be kept down. comments.name: Cinyc
comments.body:
I once asked ChatGPT whether it tailored its answers to what it knew about me. It reassured me that the facts stayed the same, then demonstrated how the same issue could be presented differently to people with different political leanings.

That reassurance now seems inadequate. Every sentence can be true while the overall account misleads through emphasis, omission and selective context. A government supporter hears the benefits; a critic hears the costs. Neither necessarily receives a false statement, but neither receives the full picture.

Personalisation should help explain the evidence, not decide which evidence we get. Using my medical background to make an explanation understandable is helpful. Using my presumed politics to make it agreeable is troubling.

The danger is that we may mistake a personalised account for an impartial one—especially when it confirms what we already believe.

How Contrastive Learning Pipelines Juxtapose Embeddings in the Age of AI

I tried on a few occasions since to figure out who gave the performance for the Evening Stars festival on the evening of Sept 9 under the World Trade Center, and could never get to the bottom of it. Nothing was published online I guess, though I contacted a handful of NY choreographers since in the past 25 years - maybe it was the repertoire of the Graham Company?

It was the most moving performance which has been with me to this day, and every time I hear Copeland I think of it. The synergy was electrifying - the dancers were flanked by the two towers soaring, my favorite buildings in NY. Seeing this, being so close to the dancing also gave way to a choking soul-crushing beauty to me somehow that night, throughout the entire performance tears streamed down my face. 

The WTC was the site of so much memorable and everlasting art because it was – as an architectural wonder and with its presence – so inexplicably full of awe.

Note that Huawei was in a joint venture with 3Com...a leading IT component biz.  That's not theft.  3Com even had a stadium naming right before it got subsumed into HP.

The history of IT telecoms is replete with competition...maybe some of it dirty...but much more so with cross licensing and joint projects.

comments.name: Nogi Ichida
comments.body:
What’s the point of having this trial? Huawei has become a global technology giant in areas far beyond telecommunications. The U.S. bans and sanctions certainly hurt the company, but they also pushed Huawei to develop capabilities it might otherwise have taken much longer to build,  from green energy and autonomous driving to battery management systems, advanced chip R&D and production, and consumer electronics.

The U.S. probably did not intend to create this outcome, but Huawei has become a landmark symbol of Chinese technological resistance, ingenuity, and resilience.

We are also seeing some countries in the West quietly scale back restrictions on Huawei equipment, simply because there are few realistic replacements from American or European suppliers. Outside the Western market, the opportunity is even bigger essentially a blue ocean for Huawei.

All of this is to say that Huawei is a remarkable technology company. Whatever one thinks about the company politically, its ability to survive sanctions, rebuild its supply chains, and expand into entirely new industries is genuinely extraordinary.

Entered Berkeley in '64 and fell into reporting about the Free Speech Movement for the campus paper, the Daily Californian. Suddenly our campus demonstrations were the focus of National News.
Meanwhile, the BIG Game was coming up--Our annual football game against Stanford. And the Pep Squads went crazy that year. Berkeley had a Civil War cannon that they fired off when our team made a touchdown. It was kept in the athletic department so it was fairly easy for the Stanford guys to steal it and haul it off. Our guys then found where it was stashed and stole it back. We are talking about a one and a half ton cannon. And sneaking it off campuses unseen. 
The Stanford guys came back to Cal and stole it again from where it had been hidden in the student union, an all glass building on the first floor.
So--our guys got mad and snuck onto Stanford and stole their two ton bell out of their bell tower.
My friend, another Daily  Cal reporter, went with the Cal guys when a truce was called and the two pep squads agreed to an exchange.Two huge trucks agreed to meet on a back country road--and kids on both sides were packing pistols and rifles. They managed to make the exchange without shooting anyone, but my friend said it was tense and scary. Over a football game, while most of our campus was embroiled in demonstrations and arrests over the change in campus rules about Free Speech on campus.

Several previous mass extinctions were caused by disruptions in long-term carbon cycles, like today.

Over hunting and fishing, habitat loss, invasive species, pollution and now climate change.

None of these things happen in a vacuum, but there are synergies among them which make the whole vastly greater than the sum of the parts.

comments.name: Erik Frederiksen
comments.body:
The last place that I lived in California was in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada near Yosemite National Park, I lived there from around 2017-2021. And we loved to backpack in the high Sierra.

But you more and more had to change outdoor plans when the wind shifted and turned the sky hazy or orange. Day time temperatures in the summer would often exceed 100F, it was a dry heat, but still hot. 

We used an evaporative cooler to cool the house, these work in dry climates by sucking a lot of air into the house through wet membranes that use evaporation to cool the air. Evaporative coolers use less energy than air conditioning and add humidity to the very dry air, an added benefit. We could get the house down to the high 70s on hot days (over 100F degrees  or 38C.)

But we started experiencing more and more wildfire smoke. You could not operate the cooler when the wind brought the smoke to your town. And when it’s really hot outside that becomes a problem.

Neighbors wells started going dry and they started getting letters from their insurance agencies, that they were being dropped due to wildfire risk. We had a good well, but the last year we were there our home insurance jumped from around $2,500/year to over $4,000.

We saw the writing on the wall. You may get a few years here and there of some relief but the trend decade to decade is hotter, more extreme drought, more extreme wildfire behavior.
